Mr. Rainville in the Chair.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
When the committee
reported last night we had just passed section 4; section 5 had already been passed. Subclause 3 of section 6 was allowed to stand pending further suggestion as to how the board of selection might be made up. The suggestion was made by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) that the local or provincial boards might have sole control for their own provinces; that instead of establishing one board we should establish nine-or really eleven', to take care of the Yukon and North West Territories. We hardly think that could work out. It is suggested, subject to any further suggestions which may be made, that this board of selection consist of say four members from' the province of Ontario, four
32S6

members from the province of Quebec, and two members from each of the other provinces. In the carrying out of the work outlined, the recommendations of the members from the provinces would be taken as to each province, but the report of the board would be the report of the whole board, which would make it much more simple than if we were to have the reports of nine boards. The boards could consist of members or senators, or those who are neither members nor senators. That is the suggestion of the Government in the matter, but if there is anything that will improve on it we will be glad to hear it.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Does my hon. friend stand by the present disposition of the Bill to have one of the members of the board appointed by the Senate and the House of Commons?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: To have them appointed by ,a joint resolution of the Senate and House of Commons, but of course to be appointed in such a way that one from each province, except Ontario and Quebbc, will be selected by the Opposition in the Senate and in the House. In Ontario and in Quebec the Opposition will select two in each, the same principle applying to the Government side in the Senate" and in the House.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: As my hon. friend is aware, I voted against this Bill, and am not much in sympathy with it. If I wanted to carry out my own views, I , think I would favour the recommendation of the Government, because, as I understand it, it is an impediment in the way of the Bill. If you have a selective board appointed by the two Houses of Parliament, it can only act when Parliament is in session, and should there be a vacancy in the board it could not be filled until the ensuing session. I do not object to that at all.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
That can be easily
cured by the resolution.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: What resolution could you frame that would cure it?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: There would have to be a resolution empowering them to sit and act when Parliament is not in session.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
But you appoint two men by resolution of the two Houses of Parliament. Suppose the two men died, or are prevented from acting, how are they to be replaced by another 
resolution of Parliament if Parliament is not in session. So far as I am concerned, I do not object to this impediment in the way of the Bill. I would suggest you might have^ one of the members of the tribunal appointed by the judicial authority, in fact I see no reason at all why the two members should not be so appointed. The chief justice, or the two senior justices could perform the duty. Yesterday I heard the compliment which was paid the judiciary by the Solicitor General, and the compliment he paid the late Government in respect to its appointments, and I feel that the chief justice in each province could perform that duty as well as anybody.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: There are objections to that, and they have been given some consideration in the course of the preparation of the Bill. I think the better course for the present would be to let clause 3 still stand, and possibly the Prime Minister might consult with the leader of the Opposition on the subject.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I have given my view.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Another point that might be considered is: what becomes of those appointees on the dissolution of Parliament.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
The appointment will be made by Parliament under such a resolution or such legislation as would provide that the appointees should not cease their functions when Parliament dissolves. The rest of the clause passed with the exception of subsection 5, which remained over at the request of the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham), with a view to. the imposition of a penalty of imprisonment. I think the suggestion is a good one, as I intimated at the time. Subsection 5 provides:
Any person duly appointed a member of a local tribunal shall, unless relieved in writing: by the authority appointing him, perform his duty as such member, and any person who without reasonable excuse fails so to do, shall be guilty of an offence and liable on summary conviction to a penalty not exceeding five hundred dollars.
It was pointed out that this might lead a man to purchasing himself out of performing this duty. I think the same objection might exist if an alternative penalty were provided, consequently I beg to move:	,
That for the words "a penalty not exceeding five hundred dollars" there be substituted the following words: "imprisonment for any

term not exceeding two years and not less than three months."

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
I thought my hon.
friend said five years last night.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: No. Five years is the penalty for refusing to report.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Do I understand that the fine is to be replaced by imprisonment?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Then I would suggest we should be disqualified.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
The suggestion does
not appeal to me at the present. I do not think members of parliament should ask, any more than any one else, to be relieved of duty in connection with the war.

no doubt that the error is in the punctuation of the French version. I do not see *why there should be the word " combatant." There is no doubt that the -section as drafted

que cela lui est dfefendu.

gentlemen to attribute the difference to the -presence of the semicolon. He now states that they have also omitted the translation of the word " and." The English version is

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Before taking up the amendments to clause 7, I would ask the Solicitor General if he does not think there should be some modification of clause 2 of section 3, which reads:-
For the purposes of this section any man married after the 11th of June, 1917, shall he deemed to he unmarried.
Does he not think it would be advisable to give the tribunal power of exemption if a marriage had been arranged prior to that date, although actually consummated afterwards? Would it not be better to leave some discretion in the tribunal?
'Mr. MEIGHEN: We shall have to return to this clause, as it has not been adopted, and in the meantime I shall consider the suggestion.	.
Mr. MoCKANEY: Has the minister considered the suggestion of the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell), that a county or district court judge should be a member of each tribunal, instead of the nominee of the judge?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
That has been very carefully considered, but it is not deemed practicable. There m-ay be cases where there is only one judge in a county, and he would

not be 'able to attend to the duties of the tribunal except in his own district.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Is there anything in the law to provide that members of local tribunals must be residents of the province in which they are to serve?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: There is no provision as to where they shall reside, but no one except those who reside in the district could perform the duties. We have sought to avoid divisions by districts, as we do not want to have any questions of jurisdiction.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: If <a man is not required to reside in the province in which he is to act, a man from Nova. Scotia might be named to serve in British Columbia.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I would not say that was legally impossible under the Bill, but it would be manifestly impossible for such a man to perform the duties, and he would never be 'appointed.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Should you not restrict appointments to local tribunals to men residing in each county?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I do not think it is necessary owing to the men who make the appointments, the judges on the one hand and a board of selection named by this Parliament on the other.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Are there any special qualifications required of the men who are to serve on local tribunals?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: None are named in the Bill. The qualifications are good common sense and strength of character.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: A man might Ibe taken from Ontario and appointed to serve in Quebec, or vice versa. Does the minister not think that, in the interests of the law, it should be provided that the men appointed should possess the respect of the community in which they reside and be known as equitable and fair-minded men, rather than to 'bring strangers from outside?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
If it were necessary to insert a provision in the Act to produce that result, we might consider framing a clause; but, on account of the authority which names the members of the tribunal, the county court judge on one hand, and the Board of Selection of Parliament on the other, who might perhaps name members of Parliament on one side or members on the other, it would seem to me rather ridiculous to suggest that they might name men who had not the respect of the public, 
and that these men should be enjoined by Parliament against sending men from Ontario into Quebec, or vice versa. Such a thing seems to me utterly inconceivable.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: The objection of the hon. gentleman from Bonaven-ture is certainly remote-rather academic than practical. At all events, he is objecting to the vicious principle of the Bill, in [DOT]regard to the appointing of the local tribunals, and I submit to my hon. friend- and I think I will be supported in my view *by hon. gentlemen in the House-that the members of the local tribunal ought to be judges. The judges are appointed by this Parliament in every community to settle disputes between man and man; they are' the arbiters appointed by law to settle difficulties in a community, and, therefore, you ask the judges to appoint members of the tribunal, but you do not ask that the men who are appointed to the tribunal should be judges. In my estimation-and I submit it in all sincerity and candor-the members of that tribunal should be men who, by their profession, are acting as arbiters between man and man. These men will have to decide whether a man is to be exempted or not. They will have to decide whether a man is fitted to be in the trenches, or whether it is better that he should be left to his own avocation. Who can settle that question better than the judges appointed by the Minister of Justice? It seems to me, in the nature of things, that the members of the tribunal should 'be the local judges, who know almost everybody in the community and who are familiar with the condition of things in the district, and who have a knowledge of the men in the community. You will, of course, find men who know the country as well as the judges, but they have not had the same training.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
I am inclined to agree, that, if it be possible for them to do the work, they are the best qualified. I have in mind the county court judge of Portage la Prairie, and I cannot conceive how any one man could, in any reasonable time, take care of the work delegated upon the tribunal by the Act in that county court district. Even if the judge had nothing else to do, the district is too large, the population too great, and the applications for exemption possibly too many for the judge to deal with. It seems to me there is very great danger of practically damning the progress of the Act by such a provision. Of course, we must not frame the provision on account

of conditions in one county only. We would not refuse to adopt the suggestion, merely because there were two or three counties where it could not be applied, but I do not think, speaking generally of Canada, from what knowledge I have at the present time, that the county court judges should be fairly asked to do all the work.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: My hon. friend from Portage la Prairie admits that the best qualified man in his district would be the county court judge, but he says that the county judge is so busy that he has no time to attend to the duties "which would be assigned to him under this Act, and, therefore, we must go to some one else. To whom shall we go? There is probably a merchant in the town, a very fine man, and quite competent, but he himself is too busy with his own business to be able to attend to it. Or there may be other prominent men who would be competent to do the work, but they are too busy in their own business. You will have to get somebody who will make the sacrifice.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: We could appoint several men, and they would take time to hold their meetings.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: You could appoint several men, and if judges are to be had, they should be appointed, and if there are no judges available, appoint some one else.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
We are making precedents all the time, and I have a practical suggestion which might work out. In every community, there is a first-class lawyer who could act as judge, and release the judge for this work. Let him be appointed as a judge, for the time being, while the judge is performing this work.
Mr. .MEIGHEN: That might be practical, if one tribunal composed of a judge could do all the work of a county. I have stated really all that I am in a position to state on that subject.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Can the hon. gentleman
tell us what was done in England?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
They did not appoint
judges at all. They had large local tribunals, composed of laymen. They did not find it possible to appoint judges there.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
All the work of these
tribunals will be subject to correction by the judges, so that you have the supervising and controlling influence of the judges, to correct errors that may occur from lack of experience on the part of members of the
tribunal. Therefore we think that, in the most practical and effective way, we avail ourselves of the undoubted competent services of the judges.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
It is stated
that appeals are never to be encouraged. I should like to see such a class of tribunals that appeals would be limited, as much as possible. If you have a class of tribunals!, in the first instance, whose composition leads you to think that it is necessary to make provision for an appeal, that is a poor arrangement.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
If we could absolutely avoid appeals, it would be a desirable thing from many points of view, but I think that would be very difficult. The best of judges are liable to err, and it would be an unfortunate situation if any number of men found themselves subjected to the judgment of one individual, without any opportunity whatever of rectifying any possible error that might creep in. I think, to meet that, we must provide for a system where there shall be a right of appeal, and if we do that, I come back to what I said before, that I think we get the best service from the judges by giving them supervision and control to rectify any mistake that may be made in the tribunal of first instance. I may s.*y that, while the questions to be determined are of very great importance, in view of the results of that determination to the individual affected and to the country, the questions, as a rule, would not be questions involving, or necessitating for their decision, any very profound knowledge of law. The question that will arise in a large number of cases, will be purely questions of fact-such 'questions as, in a great many provinces, it is thought well to leave to the decision of laymen, that is to jurors.
In many of the provinces, including our own, it is thought better, even when we have the judge, sitting there in the court, that questions of fact should be determined by laymen. It is difficult to see what questions of law will arise before these tribunals; certainly the bulk of the questions arising will be questions of fact that could he fairly dealt with by men of practical common sense. I am sure that we could repose in those men the same confidence that the law reposes in jurors, even in preference to judges.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
My hon. friend's argument would surely not apply to Ontario, where almost every county has two' county court judges. One of those judges could be re-



leased from his ordinary work in order that he might (perform the work required by this Act.
Mr. DOHERTY; In some counties in Ontario the work of the county -court judge is not very considerable; in others it is. But it must be remembered that we shall have to have more than one tribunal for each county; if the county court judge has to be on every tribunal, we cannot have more than one tribunal per county. Having regard to the population of the counties in Ontario, I fancy that it would take a long time to have all applications dealt with by one and the same tribunal. It would be anomalous to make such distinction's between the character of the tribunals that in the same county some persons would be applying to a tribunal presided over by a county court judge and others would have their cases dealt with by tribunals of another character. When you have county court judges on the tribunals, you limit the number of tribunals available for the purpose of hearing such appeals as may arise. The inadequacy of the number of judges is a very substantial objection to our constituting these tribunals of judges only. As I have said, the questions which will arise will not be such as to call for training in the law, except in exceptional instances. In those exceptional instances, if any error be committed, there will be ample remedy by appeal to the judges who under this system will be 'available for the work of correction.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Is it pro-posed that the
evidence -heard before the local tribunals shall be taken down by stenographers?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: No, I do not think that is in contemplation.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Then in what manner will it be possible for the judges in appeal to decide upon questions of fact if there is no factum before the court for decision?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Appeals of this kind will be dealt with as appeals in criminal cases are dealt with. That, in- effect, means that the appellant tribunal will hear the evidence and re-try the case.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
I think it is important that county court judges be retained as members of the local tribunals. I am in favour of having the county court judge himself act or preside rather than that he should appoint some one else for that purpose. The suggestion of the member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) is a good
[Mr. Ross.l
one. In Ontario, and, I fancy, in 'all the other provinces, in cases where the judge desires to be relieved for a time from his official duties, there is power to appoint a practising barrister of certain qualifications to attend to the judicial work of the county while the judge is absent or otherwise engaged. If a county court judge, undertaking the work assigned to him under this Act, should find that the additional work is too much for him, it would be an excellent thing to give him power to appoint some one to perform his judicial duties while he is thus engaged. Perhaps a special regulation would have to be made in regard to Quebec; certainly the law in Ontario works very well. In many cases judges obtain leave of absence for periods of three or six months and a barrister of good standing in the county is appointed to take his place. I do not think that in any instance in Ontario, unless it be in Toronto, is a county court judge overworked. I know of no junior or senior county court judge in the province who does more than four or five days' work a month. I think, therefore, that so far as Ontario is concerned there will be no difficulty in having a county court judge act in all cases-though conditions may be different in other provinces. Perhaps a general rule might be established that would clear up the whole difficulty. If I had been here when the clause was under discussion a day or two ago, I would have suggested that the tribunals in Ontario should consist of the county court judges and the wardens of the respective counties. I think that arrangement would be fair, having regard to the political parties and to every other consideration that has to be had in mind in connection with this Bill. I do not know what the municipal institutions are in the other provinces or -how such an arrangement might affect them; in any case, I think that the county court judge should himself preside over the local tribunals and that he should not have power to delegate his authority to another.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
The member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) contemplates that there will be only one tribunal for each county court district. I feel quite sure that more will be necessary in very many county court districts. Further, assuming ail ne says to be correct, a county court judge can be appointed, and I think would be appointed, by the board of selection in such a case as he has in mind. Assuming that in Ontario the county court judges all have time to perform these duties, the board of

selection can name them in every case in which they do not name themselves. In any event, this clause stands, on account of the present position of the discussion with regard to the board of selection. I fancy, therefore, that we shall get along faster if we proceed to clause 7.
Subsection stands.
On section 7-appeal tribunals:

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: How about appeals from a tribunal one of whose members is not a county court judge?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
In connection with
section 7, the/suggestion made by the mem-her for East Middlesex (Mr. Glass) has been, in the main, accepted. I thought first that it would be possible to arrange for two county court judges always to sit in appeal if a county court judge sat on the local tribunal. The difficulty, however, is that that would necessitate, in the event of their disagreeing, provision for carrying a stated case to the central appeal judge. There did not, however, seem to be the same difficulties in the way of insisting that a higher court judge should sit in appeal wherever a county court judge sat in the local tribunal, because it would be possible for the registrar to collect the cases and so allocate them that much inconvenience would be avoided in sending higher court judges to hear the appeals. I, therefore, beg to move:
That there be added to section 7 the following proviso :
Provided that appeals from the local tribunal on which sits one or more judges shall be heard and decided by an appeal tribunal constituted of a judge of a higher court.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Is there any definition of the term " higher court?"

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I do not think one could give any simpler term, or any term that required less definition.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: The Minister of Justice is aware that a judge of the superior court in Quebec may -act as judge of the higher court in his own district, or a judge of the superior court in Montreal or Quebec pray act -as the judge of the court of criminal assizes. That is the reason why I put the question: Is there any definition of what will be considered a judge of a higher court? A judge of the superior court may one minute sit as an ordinary judge of the .superior court, and the minute after he may ascend the King's Bench for the criminal assizes, and thus become a judge of a higher court.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
I am not quite certain that a King's Bench court is. higher than a ,superior court. I had the idea that all our courts stand on a parity, although they exercise different jurisdiction. The other day I intimated that I thought, for the province of Quebec, there should be a modification in the section, so that we would make quite clear what were the courts whereof the judges should be named of this -appellate court, and I, therefore, beg to move:
That section 7 be amended by inserting after the word "tribunal" in the fifth line thereof the following words:
"In the province of Quebec one judge of the Court of King's Bench or Superior Court of said province, and in the other provinces."
The reason for that will be obvious to ail hon. members from Quebec where we have not the same judicial system as prevails in the other provinces in which there are a large number of judges, not judges of higher courts, but judges of courts with very considerable civil jurisdiction. To retain the words "any court" in the case of Quebec would leave it possible (which I think would not be desirable) that a judge of a stipendiary magistrate's court or possibly of the court of sessions might be appointed, and I think it more desirable that 4 p.m. we should keep the appointments to the two courts mentioned in my amendment. It was pointed out the other day that in the city of Montreal there is a circuit court, but it seems hardly desirable to introduce in this legislation a special system for Montreal. The other day the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) stated that the circuit court judges of Montreal have all the work they can possibly do, and to appoint circuit court judges might possibly constitute a very serious injustice to the numerous litigants who come before them and who, in the great number of cases, are of that class of persons who can ill-afford to have any unnecessary delay in disposing of their cases, or any interference with the cases that are being heard.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Suppose a case comes before a judge of the superior court of Terrebonne and a decision is arrived at, and the man appeals; will he have to take his appeal to this higher court, the Court of criminal assizes, presided, over by a judge of the same district, or will he have to go before a court of appeal in Montreal?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
If the hon. member will look at the section, he will ,see that in the province of Quebec it is not contemplated that judges of the superior court should sit on the local tribunals of the first instance.

From the preceding section the hon. gentleman will note that the local tribunals will be composed of persons who are named by a judge of the superior court. In the districts of Quebec and Montreal, where there are a number of judges serving the district, the person will be selected by the Chief Justice or the acting Chief Justice of the province, as the case may be. In the other districts, the members of the local tribunals will be named by the district judge of each district, and it is not contemplated that he will name himself, nor that a judge of the district of ^Montreal will name a superior court judge to sit on the-local tribunal.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Will there always
be a judge of the superior court on the local tribunal?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: No; it is not contemplated in any case that on the local tribunal a judge of the superior court should himself sit.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: He may sit in appeal? He will be considered as belonging to a "higher court?''

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Yes. The hon. member need not be troubled about the term "higher court." Under the amendment I have just moved, it is provided that in the province of Quebec the appellate court shall consist of one judge of the court of King's Bench, or of the superior court of the province.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Has section 7, as
printed, been passed?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: There are two amendments proposed; one by myself, which is a proviso, and the other by the Minister of Justice. Outside of that, the section is as printed in the Bill.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
There is a suggestion
I would like to make, -but I may be too late. The section reads:
The Chief Justice of the court of last resort in each province .	.	. shall establish.	.	. Appeal Tribunals-
And so on. The language is mandatory, not permissive. Then there is a reservation:
In case of his absence, or failure to act, then a judge of that court designated by the minister.
Why not "designated by the said Chief Justice?" If the minister is the proper person to. make the appointment, he should do it in the first instance.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
does not get the exact meaning. The Chief Justice is to make the appointment of the judges, who themselves will be the appeal tribunals. If he fails to act, if he fails to name those appeal tribunals, then the minister names a judge who will name them.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Why should not the
Chief Justice name that judge?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
If the Chief Justice
fails to do the one thing, the probability is that he will fail to do the other. We do not, however, contemplate any such failure except on account of physical dis-*ability or necessary absence. If any one should fail to appoint the tribunals, they would likely fail also to appoint a judge to appoint the tribunals, so we take care that the tribunals shall be appointed by giving the minister power to name some one else to take the place of the Chief Justice in case the latter fails.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I see that subsection 3 of section 6 states that the tribunals shall consist of two members. What is the meaning of the word "members"? Can an ex-convict or a woman; or a man engaged in military service be appointed a member of a local tribunal? I think the word "member" should be defined.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Surely the hon. member does not apprehend that any judge of the superior court is going to appoint to these tribunals a penitentiary convict, or a woman, or any of the classes of people whom I am sorry to see my hon. friend grouping together. If we had to define what kind of a man is to be appointed I think it would lead us into giving a great many details. If we put the appointing power in the hands of the most competent and reliable people we can find, I think we can trust to their judgment to appoint the right class of people to sit on the tribunals. We have, on the one hand, the judges, and on the other, the selective board, the formation of which has not been absolutely settled, but which at all events will clearly be a body enjoying the confidence of the Senate and the House of Commons of Canada. I think under those circumstances we can be satisfied that no objectionable person will be appointed to these tribunals.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
I have confidence
in the good faith of a man, but I think it would be safe to have the word " member ' expressly defined in the Bill.
Section as amended agreed to.

On section 11-application for, and grounds of exemption:

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: This section was carried with the understanding that I should speak to the committee with regard to suggestions that had been made. One suggestion, in regard to which I wish to move an amendment, is with respect to paragraph (f)-the "conscientious objectors" clause. It was urged that an earlier date should be fixed than the date of the passing of this Act regarding the existence of religious denominations opposed to military service. I therefore beg to move that for the words "at the date of the passing of this Act" there be substituted "on the 6th of July, 1916."

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: What religious denominations will be exempt? Will a man be exempt who declares before a tribunal that he cannot conscientiously take arms for the killing of another human being?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: What the Bill requires is not merely that a man shall have conscientious objections to military service, but that he be prohibited from combatant service by the tenets and articles of faith, in effect at the date of the passing of this Act, of any organized religious denomination existing and well recognized in Canada. Now the questions, what are the tenets and articles of faith, and what is an organized religious denomination well recognized in Canada, are all matters of fact susceptible of proof otherwise than by the mere statement of the applicant.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: A man, then, will have no right to decide according to his conscientious beliefs?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
He can decide his conscientious beliefs for himself, but in order that he should be entitled to exemption it is required not merely that he himself should conscientiously object, but that he should be a member of a religious organization well recognized in Canada whose tenets prohibit his acting as a combatant.
So he has two things to prove: not only the state of his own conscience, but the further fact that the state of his conscience is the result of his conforming to the tenets of any organized and well recognized religious denomination existing in the country at the time mentioned.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in order to be better understood, I shall speak in French to submit the following point:
I find that the English statute does not go as far as the Bill now before us. Why should we exempt the .party claiming as an exemption the fact that he belongs to any religious sect whatever, and why could no't the judge hearing the applicant's objections consider the conscientious motives of another party claiming the same exemption?
We already have in the law of evidence in the province of Quebec and generally in the Canadian law of evidence exemptions of this nature. For example, if a man refuses to take an oath upon the Bible he is allowed to be sworn in some other way, or to make a solemn affirmation, and his scruples are recognized and respected.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
I have previously pointed out that, under this Act, it is not only required that the applicant objects to serve as a soldier on conscientious grounds, but, moreover, that he actually belongs to a church or religious sect whose tenets forbid all its adherents to serve as soldiers.
The tribunal undoubtedly will implicitly believe whatever he states as to his beliefs, but when it comes to determine the two other facts, firstly, whether he belongs to a certain religious sect, and, secondly, whether the tenets of that same sect forbid his serving as a soldier, I do not believe that it would be fair to allow.him by means of this only statement in the form of a yes or a no what prohibitions do exist according to the rules and regulations of that religious sect. This is a fact readily proven, because it must be remembered that it applies only to religious obligations generally established and recognized in this country. As for the case recalled by the hon. member, when you only have to know what is a man's belief, he is perfectly free to state it. But here you need a further fact, which is quite independent of his own beliefs, and is, as a matter of fact, to be proven independently of his own statement.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
In Montreal very recently, they went pretty far; they

refused to accept the oath of a witness who had refused to give it on the Bible, because he had declared he did not believe in God. His belief was to that extent respected.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: His belief shall be duly respected, in accordance with the prohibitions of the church [DOT]or religious denomination to which he belongs.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Would the hon. minister allow me a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Certainly.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: We have in some of our classical colleges ecclesiastics, some of whom are in the minor orders, others in the major ones. What I want to know is whether an ecclesiastic who has only received the tonsure, which according to our church is a real order, is, under the Act, exempted from military service?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I may inform my hon. friend that the word "clergy" in this Bill comprises every one who has received holy orders, and that the tonsure is an order.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
It is very easy to
see in reading this section that the questions which will be decided by the tribunals will be simply questions of fact. The local tribunals will have to decide whether it is expedient in the national interest that a man should be employed in the military service or in any other work, or whether his exceptional financial or domestic situation prevents him from going to the front. That is absolutely a question of fact. As every one knows, the decisions of lower courts on questions of fact are never reversed by the higher courts, unless gross injustice has been committed. Why then so man$r appeals? In the first place we have the local tribunal, in which a judge may sit because the Solicitor General told us that if the judge is not very busy in his district he may be appointed to serve on the tribunal. The decision of this local tribunal as to whether a man shall or shall not go to the front will then be confirmed or reversed by the higher court on the same question of fact. Even that is not sufficient, 'because he may have to go before the Supreme Court, where one man may reverse the decision of three or four others who have seen and heard the witnesses and who are personally acquainted with the circumstances of the particular case. I really believe that this provision is inflicting a great hardship on

those who will have -to go from one court to another, and it is contrary to the accepted principles of law and equity.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
But, the hon. member
forgets it is not strictly an appeal. The leader of the Opposition naised the point in the first place, and it was clearly indicated that what is allowed is of the nature of an appeal from summary conviction, and new evidence may he made; consequently it is partly in the nature of a new trial. While it is true the matter before the local tribunal is one of fact, still there may be errors in the application of the principle deciding the question of fact, and it is well that those errors should be passed upon by a man who has the training of a judge.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: But the member of the first appeal tribunal has the training of a judge. Why then go further than this appeal? Why bring the appeal to Ottawa?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
To bring it before the
Central Appeal Judge.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Why?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: With a view to securing the uniform acceptance and application of the principles. What is before the committee is an s amendment to tne effect that the date of the existence of the denominational body be fixed at, say, July 6.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Apparently some of the hon. members find objection to this clause on the ground that some fake religious organizations may be established with a view to keeping men away from the war. If the words " well recognized toy the law in Canada " be inserted, and a date fixed, it would cover the difficulty. No matter how small a religious organization may be, it must have an Act which enables 'it to hold property. This would establish it as a matter of fact, and give its members -a status before the tribunals. There are certain branches of the Socialists known as the Individualists, who might claim they are entitled to exemption under thiis law. Their existence might be recognized because of their meetings and so on, tout, to give them a status under this Bill, they should be recognized by the law.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I did not have any reference to any sect whatever. I wanted to know how far -a man's individual thought would toe considered by the law, or whether he had to belong to some particular sect or denomination

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: The Act should be made more specific in that respect, so that the onus -would not be on the tribunal to say whether some small local organization, such as may exist in various parts of the country, and which has no status whatever, should be recognized. If it is recognized by law, then there should be some organization behind it. I think possibly that would avoid all that difficulty.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
The governing test
should be the reality and bona fides of the denomination. That reality and bona fides could not be determined by the mere fact of the body having a corporate existence. There might be a very real and thoroughly sincere denomination without such a corporate existence-

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: But not recognized by law.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Not recognized by law- a body who had not gone to the trouble or had not seen any object in taking out letters of incorporation or in becoming recognized by law. That would appear to me to be an arbitrary test to apply. It is a question of fact whether such an organization really exists and is recognized.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Are the local tribunals versed in the theology of all these various sects?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: It is not a question of theology, but merely of the existence of the denomination and its recognition in the community. It is a question of fact which the local tribunals will decide in the first instance.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: My understanding is that this relates to the Mennonites, the Douk-hobors, and the Quakers.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: And the Christa-delphians.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Those would be included; there may be more.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: They are all incorporated and hold property and are well recognized organizations. I do not think the minister could mention any organization with an article of this kind in its creed that is not already recognized by law and has not its chapels. Those who are not in that position are those who cannot come out in the light of day and show themselves. I do not think they are entitled to exemption.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
I do not think that even so outstanding a body as the Quakers have any incorporation. There may be individuals incorporated as a church, but I
think it would be risky to say that every sect of Quakers in Canada, wherever located, have legal incorporation; but, even if one could say that, it would be more risky to say that every other body entitled to exemption has incorporation.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Has my hon. friend in mind the same exemption that is provided for in the Militia Act, or is this section entirely new and introduced with a view of exempting other persons than those who were mentioned or entitled to be mentioned in the Militia Act?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: The experience in Great Britain would go to show that it would be very dangerous to accept the wording of the Militia Act as it now reads. That leaves out the persons who, from the doctrines of their religion, are averse to bearing arms or rendering military service under such conditions as may be specified. My hon. friend would hardly suggest that the matter could safely be left in that form.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Did I understand that the Christian Brothers were to be exempted?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I did not specify any denominations.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: There are a number of Christian Brethren in my constituency, and I would like to know whether they are to be exempted or not.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: That will be cleared up by the proper tribunal.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: What has been the actual experience in England under the last conscription law? I see that the conscientious objectors are exempt. Does that include certain sects, or are individuals who do not belong to any specified sect exempted?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Under the first Act as it was introduced a man was able to secure exemption merely by convincing the tribunal of his own individual predisposition in the matter. The application of the law had to be tightened, as they found that the number who conscientiously objected to going to the war was very large indeed. This section embodied the good points of both the British and the United States sections.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the Solicitor General was to take into consideration an amendment moved by yourself (Mr. Rainville) to subclause (a), with re-

ference to agriculture. Did he take that into his consideration?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
It was moved by the hon. member for Chambly-Vereheres (Mr. Rainville) that there be added after the word "in" in the third line of (a) "agricultural, industrial or." Objection was taken by the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) that the effect would be to require the interpretation of the word "other" oil the principle of ejusdem generis, and consequently to imperil the right of those engaged in such occupations as transportation to secure exemption. Whether those engaged in transportation and similar occupations would be shut out by the principle of ejusdem generis is a question which it might now be perilous to raise. Take teachers in schools and institutions,
should be afraid that the principle of ejusdem generis would shut out their right to secure exemption.
of my hon. friend were accepted, it would not make any difference in any other work. I would not say the duties of a school teacher should not be called work, because sometimes he has pretty heavy work.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
His duty means work ail right, but, agriculture rand industry are mentioned .specifically. The other work would need to be of the same nature and kind-ejusdem generis-as industrial work: consequently, teachers might be excluded. As to the third British Act, I think, if the hon. gentleman will read the title to the Act, and the preamble, he will see that it has not the effect, or the wide application, he thinks it has. The title is:
An Act to enable the exception from military service of men excepted on the ground of previous rejection, or the previous relinquishment of, or discharge from, naval or military service, or unsuitability for foreign service, to be reviewed.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: They would come under (c.)

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
No, they are not in
training; they are training. Then there is this objection, that notwithstanding the very strong claims of agriculture, speaking generally, to exemption, which claim doubtless will result in adequate exemptions for agriculture, the same argument could be made for the classes suggested by Mr. Girard, say those engaged in fisheries,-who are producers of a food more and more required by reason of war conditions, and other similar industries might be particularized. Consequently it was thought that, especially since this clause has worked satisfactorily in Great Britain under this wording, it would be better to keep it in its present form.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
The clause in the British Act specially mentions agriculture, if I read it correctly. Speaking of the exemptions, the section says:
Provided also that the powers under thi: provision shall not extend-
(a) to any man who is for the time beim engaged in agriculture, and whose work i: certified by the Board of Agriculture anc Fisheries (or, as respects Scotland, the Board of Agriculture for Scotland) to De work ol national importance, and who was engaged on such work on the thirty-first day ol -t larch, nineteen hundred and seventeen.
When my hon. friend suggested it, he did so because in the interpretation it specially mentioned agriculture and did not mention anything else. So far as I can see by this clause, if the suggestion 
The Act proceeds:
Be it enacted by the King's Most Excellent Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and Commons, in this present Parliament assembled, and by the authority of the same.
Then it is provided that the powers under this provision shall not be extended to any man who is, for the time being, engaged in agriculture, and so forth. It has not the effect of exempting agriculture from the general provisions of the Act. It simply says that, in this combine at this stage, there shall be these exceptions. I may not have stated it as strongly as I should have, from my standpoint, but, at any rate, I have not stated it too strongly.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I did not understand my hon. friend to propose that agriculture should be excluded altogether. I only meant that it should be emphasized in the exception.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before the exemption clause is finally adopted, I would like to again express my regret that the 'Government have not seen fit to accept the suggestion offered by some of the members in order to exempt the farmers from compulsory military service. After all that has been said in this House,
I am led to understand, that under subsection (a) every one or almost any one can be exempted from military service; I believe the. hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) has thus expressed himself. I perfectly understand that the farmers may be placed under this head, but at .all events, they will be no less under the obligation of

appearing before some tribunal within a certain delay, just as will be the case for all men between twenty and fonty-five years o.f age, while, if a general exemption had 'been provided for in the Act itself, they (would have been relieved of such an obligation. Moreover, this obligation cannot but entail numerous inconveniences, specially if this Act should be enforced during harvest time. Some members have expressed the opinion that such a clause would be an insult to the agricultural class. To me this argument does not seem a serious one, inasmuch as our farmers are not over scrupulous on the subject, and that they could enlist anyway whenever they saw fit. The farmers are so necessary in Canada that they should not be enticed to enlist in any way whatever.
I now want to draw the attention of the House to a charge which has been laid here by three members, a charge we ought to investigate as I believe.
I stated when I spoke in this House on June 27 ultimo that I had heard that a large number of young Englishmen had emigrated to Canada during the first months of the war in order to evade compulsory military service enacted in England. The hon. member for Montcalm (Mr. Lafortune) made the same assertion in this House on July 5th, last Thursday. I will quote his own words:
Frequently, we see steamers coming into port with some 700 or $(00 young Englishmen on board; we see them strutting, with a new walking stick, along the streets of Montreal. They come over to our country to fill the places of our French Canadian boys who are expelled from our stores and our mills, in order to force them, in a sense, to enlist.
At this point the hon. member for L'Islet (Mr. Paqnet) interrupted the hon. member for Montcalm and asked him:

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Will the hon_ member allow me one question?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Certainly.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Has the hon. member information to justify his assertion that the French Canadians are replaced in the munition factories by Englishmen just come from the British Isles?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Certainly, I am not afraid to assert it.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: The charge is a most serious one.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Most
serious, I admit it; hut I do, nevertheless, declare that, in many cases, French Canadians are turned out of doors and that their places are given, a few days later, to your Englishmen just landed from London. The very thing happened in a shell factory In my own village; these French Canadians were told: " Why don't you enlist? Why don't you go and help the Empire"? They were thus forced to sacrifice themselves
and to give up all they held most dear, in order to save the Empire.
Now, I read in the Hansard of the 11th instant, another almost similar charge laid by the hon. member for Cbambly-Vercheres (Mr. Rainville) when he stated that some
73.000	men, after enlisting in the Canadian Army, deserted and disappeared.
He added, that the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), referring to a Detroit newspaper, stated that it had been ascertained that 17,000 English Canadians, mostly from Ontario, were living in that city. Headed:	"We have some slackers
here from England to be found in insurance offices in Montreal"-And, more than that, relying on statistics which he must have had from good authority, he said that the immigration which had bad figured up to
43.000	men in 1914, I believe, had reached 85,000, in 1916, which means an increase of
42.000	for 1916. That is surely an extraordinary fact, and the hon. member for Chambly-Vercheres stated:	"I would
strongly urge that these slackers who have gone to the United States should be brought back."
In both cases which I have just quoted, 1 believe there is for the Government ample justification for a searching investigation, and that would be of primary importance. These facts appear to me far more important than the charge made against people of the province of Quebec of having insulted soldiers -on their way through. Now, I do believe that the charge laid against these deserters and these emigrants who have left their country in order to evade military service, is far more serious than the other I have just aliuded to; it would be only right, it seems to me, that the Government should make an investigation upon it.

speechtext:
I took the liberty of discussing this clause at some length on a previous occasion. I now desire to take advantage of the copy of the United States law, which was laid on the Table, for the purpose of supporting and emphasizing the position I took in regard to what was to me the evident purpose of this section, and which was not related to a fair conscription of the man-power of the country. The parallel section of the United States Act reads as follows:
Kec. 4. That the Vice-President of the United States, the officers, legislative, executive and judicial, of the United States, and of the several States, Territories, and the District of Columbia, regular or duly ordained ministers of religion, students who at the, time of the approval of this Act are preparing for the ministry in recognized theological or divinity schools, and all persons in the military and naval service of the United States, shall be exempt from the selective draft herein prescribed; and nothing in this Act contained shall be construed to require or compel any person to serve in any forces herein provided for who is found to he a member of any well-recognized religious sect or organization at present organized and existing and whose existing creed or principles forbid its members to participate in war in any form, and whose religious convictions are against war or participation therein in accordance with the creed or principles of said religious organizations, but no person so exempted shall he exempted from service in any capacity that the President shall declare to be non-combatant; and the President is hereby authorized to exclude or discharge from said selective draft and from the draft under the second paragraph of section 1 hereof for partial military service only from those liable to draft as in this Act provided persons of the following classes:	County and municipal
officials; customhouse clerks; persons employed by the United States in the transmission of the mail; artificers and workmen employed in the armouries, arsenals, and- navy

yards of the United States, and such other persons employed in the service of the United States as the President may designate; pilots; mariners actually employed in the sea service of any citizen or merchant within the United States; persons engaged in industries, including agriculture, found to he necessary to the maintenance of the military establishment or the effective operation of the military forces, or the maintenance of national interest during the emergency; those in a status with respect to persons dependent upon them for support which renders their exclusion or discharge advisable; and those found to be physically or morally deficient. No exemption or exclusion shall continue when a cause therefor no longer exists.
It will be observed that this provision of the United States Act covers, in a great measure, the same exemptions as are covered specifically in this provision of section XI of the Act we are considering, but it differs from section 11 on the very points I raised, and in support of which I expressed myself somewhat strongly. The conditions, of the United States being more closely parallel to those in Canada I think we might fairly look to the law of the United States for guidance in dealing with our conditions here; and as the legislators of the United States had the advantage of the British law, and reached the conclusion they did-a conclusion that is vastly different in its operation from the law we are now discussing-I contend that my position has very good support.
The first difference between section 11 and this provision of the United States 'Act to which I wish to draw attention is that there is a very much greater specification of exemption. I impressed upon the hon. minister the desirability of making more specific exemptions. He refused to make those exemptions, and demanded that I should give him even one exemption. I have quoted from the United States Act, and he is at liberty to consider that all the exemptions in the United States Act would be proper exemptions to be included in our Act.
The next difference to which I wish to draw attention is that in the United States Act there is no provision parallel to paragraph (b) of subsection 1, section 11, a provision of our Act, which I have taken the liberty pf saying has been inserted in the Bill for the purpose of using the threat of compulsory military service, as a means of securing labour for friends of the Government- engaged in industrial enterprises in Canada. There is no such provision in the United States Act.
The other feature I desire to draw attention to is that the tribunals organized under the United States Act are subject in their decisions to regulations framed by the Pre-

sident. They will be directed by the responsible authorities of the country, and I am one of those old-fashioned people believe in responsible government. I 'believe in the Government of our country being responsible for its acts of administration, particularly so where life and liberty and right are at stake. The efforts of the Bill to 'divest our Government of responsibility fpr whatever action may be taken by the tribunals is not a policy that appeals to my mind as being sound from any point of view, and I direct the attention of the House to the fact that it is not the system adopted in the United States. The President of the United States is held responsible for the regulations under which exemptions will be granted by the local tribunals.
Another difference is that certain of the exemptions are to be dealt with by what might be called the inferior tribunals. Another class of exemptions is to be dealt with by what we will call the appeal tribunals only. The reason for that distinction is very obvious, and I maintain that it is a wise distinction. I shall read the provision :
The President is hereby authorized, in his descretion, to create and establish throughout the several States and subdivisions thereof and in the territories and the District of Columbia local boards, and where, in his discretion, practicable and desirable, there shall be created and established one such board in each county or similar subdivision in each State, and one for approximately each thirty thousand of population in each city of thirty thousand population or over, according to the last census taken or estimates furnished by the Bureau of Census of the Department of Commerce. Such boards shall be appointed by the President, and shall consist of three or more members, none of whom shall be connected with the military establishment, to he chosen from among the local authorities of such subdivisions or from other citizens residing in the subdivision or area in which the respective boards will have jurisdiction under the rules and regulations prescribed by the President. Such boards shall have power within their respective jurisdictions to hear and determine, subject to review as hereinafter provided, all questions of exemption under this Act, and all questions of or claims for including or discharging individuals or classes of individuals from selective draft, which shall be made under rules and regulations prescribed by the President, except any and every question or claim for including or excluding or discharging persons or classes of persons from the selective draft under the provisions of this Act authorizing the President to exclude or discharge from the selective draft "Persons engaged in industries, including agriculture, found to be necessary to the maintenance of the military establishment, or the effective operation of the military forces, or the maintenance of national interest during the emergency."

The exceptions are those that come directly before the appeal tribunal and are not tried before the original tribunal at all. From beginning to end the purpose of the United States Act is plain on its face. That purpose is to raise so many men, to raise them on a basis of population, and to raise them with the object of finding men for the fighting line. It is because the Bill before the House differs from the United States Bill in those particulars that I, as a member of this House, object to it, and object to it most strongly. 1 took the liberty of saying that in my opinion the provisions of the Bill as we have it before us were as they were with the distinct idea in the mind of the Government not to administer the Bill with a view to laying an. equal burden of service upon all the people of Canada, and I further took the liberty of saying that that was made absolutely evident by the fact that no provision was contained in the Bill requiring such equality of service. I have read to the House the section of the American Act regarding exemptions. But the section concludes with a proviso as follows:
Provided, that notwithstanding the exemptions enumerated herein, each State, Territory, and -the District of Columbia shall be required to supply its quota in the proportion that its population bears to the total population of the United States.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
I need not refer to the portions of the hon. gentleman s speech which were repetitions of his stand previously taken. The UnJited States legislation makes certain specific exceptions, just as ours makes certain specific exceptions, and much along the lines of our exceptions in the schedules. It then proceeds to authorize the President to make more exceptions it does not make them-and included in the further exceptions which the President is authorized to make are pilots, mariners, and a great many people, and then persons engaged in industry, including agriculture, found to be necessary to the maintenance of the military establishment and the effective operation of the military forces or the maintenance of the national interest during the emergency. Then it provides that notwithstanding such exceptions that may thus be made, or may not he made, the men must be secured, so that if the securing of the men invades the exemptions the men have to be obtained all the same. What is the difference between that and ours? We also say that we exclude industries essential for the national interest, and we say that we exclude them only to such an extent as will enable us to get the men. 'What is the
real fundamental difference there? Does any one suggest that we in Canada should say that all engaged in industries beneficial to the national interest shall be excused? Does any one say that, out of mere idlers left in Canada, doing nothing, engaged in no industry whatever for the national interest, we could pick up the 100,000 men fit for military service, physically fit. No one would suggest that. We would have to do as they provide for here, if enough men were not secured without invading the exemptions then you would have to invade industries, first those not essential and then those essential. So, in effect, it is the siame. They establish tribunals to determine these things and do not say that the President shall exempt these men; they simply authorize him to do so. It is true that we have responsible Government here and it has a fairly faithful adherent in myself, so much so that on questions of very great and insistent responsibility I think it is the province of the Government to discharge that responsibility and not shift it to the people, not try to relieve itself of the responsibility. Such is my adherence to the principle of responsible government. But .the principle of responsible government is not impaired by leaving to the judicial authorities the determination of questions of law and fact, nor, I submit again, is it impaired by leaving to the jury of tribunals simple questions of fact such as are left to them by this Bill.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.

speechtext: Will a man be given a certificate to show that he has reported?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: This provision applies, I suppose, to the case of men who desire to he exempted on the ground that by reason of age they do not belong to the class called up. In a country like ours with so large a portion of our population coming from other countries, and where there is so much moving about on the part of our people, it may be very difficult for a man to produce proof of his age. Has that been taken into consideration, and what steps will be taken to meet that condition?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
My hon. friend is not,
I think, quite right in his idea that exemption is in any way related to this question. A man would not be able to go to a tribunal and say: "I, am not in that class at all; therefore, give me a certificate of exemption." If he believes that he is not in the class called, he should not go to the tribunal at all, but simply stay at home. Then if he should be prosecuted he would come and give the best evidence of his age that he could, and however difficult it might be for him to show his exact age, it would be infinitely more difficult for the Crown to show what his age was. He will be in the possession of the best evidence that is procurable, whatever that evidence mav be.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: That latter instance is what I had in mind. I am sure the minister will appreciate the difficulty that a very large part of the population of our western coun-; try would have in establishing their age before a tribunal. I do not know whether it is possible to make a provision recognizing that difficulty, which is peculiar to our country and did not exist in any degree in England.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: To a great many it would be very, very difficult to establish their age. But this must be remembered; they will try to sbow their age not before any tribunal we are establishing but before the regular courts-before the magistrate or county court judge in appeal, as the case may be-because that is where any prosecution would take place at which they would have to show their age. While they, might not be able there to show their exact age, still they would be able to give much evidence as would persuade the judge one way or the other, and if he was of the opinion that the man was really outside of the class called up I have no doubt that on the ordinary principles of law he would say: "That is a reasonable excuse, anyway," and the man would not be punished.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Suppose that A is called up but is really not in the class. He would have to furnish the best evidence he could that he was not of the age called up. In our province the best evidence would be a certificate of birth, and that costs something like a dollar. I know that from personal experience, because not very long ago I was asked by an insurance company with whom I had carried a policy for several years, to renew the evidence of my age, and I had to go to the registry office and get a birth certificate and pay for it. Where there are many young men in a community, quite a number of these certificates would be obtained from the registry office. Who is going to pay the costs?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: That is not provided for. While the production of certificates might be, I might say, final evidence, Still it is not the only evidence. A parent may swear to his son's age, and that is very strong, if not final evidence.
