On proposed new section 16-penalties:

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
I move that paragraph 1 of the new section 16 should he the following:
Any person who comes within any of the classes set out in section 3. and who contravenes any of the provisions of this Act, or regulations made thereunder, for which contraventions no other penalty is herein provided, shall be guilty of an offence, and shall be liable upon summary conviction to a penalty of not less than $100 nor more than $500, or to imprisonment for a term of not less than one month nor more than twelve months, or to both fine and imprisonment.
It will be observed that in this section as transcribed in Hansard the word "or" appears after "contraventions," and the word "and" appears after "$500." The word "or" should be "no," and the word "and" should be "or."

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: As I understand it, under this Act the penalty is always fine and imprisonment.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I think that would be the effect, as it reads.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Does not the minister think that "not less than $100" is a very severe penalty for what may be a very trivial offence? There are a great many provisions in this Act, and a person may inadvertently transgress in a small way. If the court is obliged to say that he is found guilty of any offence under the Act, there is no alternative but to fine him $100 or more. It seems to me that is rather severe. I have always been opposed to those minimum sentences. I think there should be discretion left to the courts.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Of course this is the first time the clause has been before the committee, and the Government will be very glad to hear the views of hon. members on the question of the minimum fine.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
In my judgment there is much more than that. This paragraph is most drastic. I do not believe it is possible to find in any law anything so vague, so general, and so severe. There are special penalties provided in the Act for specific offences. I have two in mind at the moment, but there are others. A man who neglects to report is liable to a fine, and a man who has not a certificate to exhibit to a peace officer is liable to a fine. Of course, I cannot find fault with the principle that there should be penalties for specific offences, but here is a penalty of $100 and an imprisonment of twelve months for a contravention of something which is not defined in the Act. Read it again, Mr. Chairman, and I will leave it to the common sense and fairness of both sides of the House. What contravention is here contemplated You have specific offences already provided for. but here is a vague

enactment that if any one contravenes something which is not defined he is liable to a fine and imprisonment. That is not fair or right; it is not justice. I cannot imagine what contravention is here contemplated, which would subject a man to a fine of $100 and imprisonment for twelve months besides.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: That is not at all an unusual type of section in a Bill. I am sure my right hon. friend will remember other Bills where a general clause is inserted providing against infractions not specifically mentioned in the Bill. I have in mind a clause in the Criminal Code, which is even a great deal more general than this. I think it was passed under my right hon. friend's Government, but of that I >am not sure. It says that any one contravening any of a certain class of laws not mentioned in the Code shall be liable to a certain penalty.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: That is disobedience of a statute.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Exactly. Such contravention renders a man guilty of an offence, and the punishment is set out. A more extreme case than that can scarcely be conceived. It does not even say what the statute is.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.

My right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) asks me what is the offence contemplated. There is no special offence contemplated, but by reference to section. 12 it will be seen that the Governor in Council has power to make regulations to secure the full effective and expeditious operation and enforcement of the Act. Under paragraph 2, subsection 1, they may appoint such peace officers, or other officers, and give them such powers, and impose on them such duties as may be deemed necessary. Under subsection (g) they may prescribe penalties for peace officers or other officers appointed under the authority of the Act, who are convicted of neglect or refusal to perform duty without reasonable excuse. They may not only prescribe penalties for refusing to perform the duty, but may also make regulations binding on the men who come within these classes.
They may make duties in connection with reporting on the nature of their exemptions, etc. But it is well to have a general clause covering it. I am not insisting on the $100 minimum; in fact, I was impressed by the

Prescribe penalties for peace officers or other officers appointed under the authority of this Act, who are convicted of neglect or refusal to perform duty without reasonable excuse.

The regulations may provide for punishment for neglect of a duty which is of a trivial nature, and then impose a penalty in accordance with that trivial offence. But here you provide a double penalty of $100 and imprisonment besides for an offence which is in the air, breach of a regulation which has not been made. The regulation may be absolutely trivial, and for the breach of that trivial regulation you have a double penalty of such a grievous character as this.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
That is a grave and serious offence. We are dealing with minor offences. Stealing from the mail is one of the most serious offences dealt with by the Code, hut hon. gentlemen opposite always have the happy faculty of passing off anything on us that may appear to have gone through this Parliament when we were in power. One of the things of which the Conservative party in the country is proud -and they have reason to be proud

is that the Right Hon. Sir John Thompson was the father of the Criminal Code, and we always gave him credit for it, so that the Liberals are not responsible for anything found in the Code. But they throw the Code at us and say, " This thing is in the Code, and so you cannot complain of it." Although we are not responsible for the paternity of the Code, we are proud of some parts of it, and have no cause to find fault with many of its provisions. If my hon. friend will run through the provisions ol the Code with reference to assault, which sometimes are of a grave character, he will find that provision is made for a fine not exceeding $20. The Code does not say it must be $5 or $6, but simply says a fine not exceeding $20, or imprisonment not exceeding three months. It tapers to nothing, on the one hand, and may go as high as $20, for the gravest kind of assault on the other hand. I submit the question can be left to the discretion of the court, up to a certain amount. I am not very particular as to what the maximum will be, but I think it will be safe to leave it to the discretion of the judge, as to whether it will he one, two. or ten dollars. I submit that, for a trivial offence, the judge's hands should not be tied, and it should not be compulsory for him to impose as high a fine as $10.

speechtext:
All that is governed by the word " induces " in the earlier part of the clause. The whole paragraph,
-or for the purpose of obstructing, hindering or impeding the operation or administration of this Act to abstain from submitting for decision of the proper tribunals claims for exemption under this Act or the evidence available in support thereof or in any manner whatsoever to embarrass the Government-
[DOT]-is governed by the phrase " persuades, induces ox influences, or attempts to persuade, induce ox influence any person or anybody ox class of persons to resist." We have tried to make it perfectly clear that the people who ATe wanted to he got at by this section are those who, I think everybody will agree, should be visited with condign punishment. This section is not aimed at, and does not strike at, the man liable to conscription, but it does strike at those who axe standing behind with no obligations of their own and with their skins perfectly safe, they may imagine. We have had a good deal of pronouncement, not only of desire but of full intention to make this an unworkable Act. This section is framed to strike at those who try to induce other people to hinder, and at those who do hinder the operation of this Act after iit has been duly enacted and come into force. To my mind that is an exceedingly grave offence; and, to suggest, because we are trying to .prevent that exceedingly grave offence-and wording the section so as to make it perfectly clear, in my humble judgment, whom it is intended to hit at-that we 'axe trying to legislate to prevent criticism of this Government seems to me to be going a little beyond the limit at all events of fair criticism of this section. I would have thought that there would have been unanimity in this House that any man or class of men who after this becomes the law of the land seek to hinder its being carried out ought to be punished. The purpose of this section is to reach that class of men, and only that class of men.

To those who are engaged in newspaper work the following section is even more applicable than the one we are now quoting, and it is very necessary in the public interest that the law be made so clear that no person can take advantage of the Act to suppress what is legitimate criticism in the public interest. No Government, or minister, or tribunal, is infallible, and unless it is made clear that the Act is not to place them above criticism by the pTess or by the speaker on the platform or in discussion, the Government, with all its goodness, and the tribunals might go astray. I have never taken the [DOT] ground in the newspapers that the bench itself was above criticism. In some cases it can be legitimately and reasonably criticised. But I want the minister to make it absolutely clear that this clause does not restrict legitimate criticism and that such criticism will not be looked upon as an offence even if it embarrasses the Government or the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
I do not know if there are words .that could make it any more clear I would be glad to make it clears'-, if 't were possible. It does not hit at criticism, legitimate or illegitimate, as long as it is kept to criticism. It is the hindering or impeding or wilful attempt to resist, obstruct, hinder or impede; or to persuade, induce, or influence other people; or to embarrass t,he Government or the minister in the carrying out of their operations. Perhaps it was not proper for me to say I thought the criticism unfair, but it is a great surprise to me, because the thought

never entered my mind that' this section affected criticism in any way. Certainly there was no intent to affect criticism in any shape. I have read it again, and I cannot see how anybody could bring " criticism " within the four corners of this section.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
There is an advantage in connection with this section, which we have not had in connection with any of the rest
of	the Act.	When	we	discussed	any	other section of	the	Act	thatwe	did not	consider	applicable	to
conditions in this country, we were told it was the Act in England, or some place else. Now we are dealing with a section for the origination of which I believe my hon. friend the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) and my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) claim to divide the credit between them. That being the case, and seeing that in no country in the world up to the present time has there been drastic enactments of this kind,-I am sure if there had been >
it would have been referred to before now-I am in agreement with my hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham), that it is entirely proper that when this Parliament is passing an Act it should take all reasonable and necessary means to secure, not only the enforcement of the Act, but a proper respect for the Act in its enforcement. So far as this provision goes, if in the wisdom of the Government it is considered necessary to make such drastic provision as this, then I have nothing to say; but I think the Government takes upon itself a grave responsibility to say that in this supposedly free country, and at this date in the history of the world, it is necessary to impose a limitation upon the right of free discussion such as we are told there is no precedent for in any other legislation my hon. friends have made themselves acquainted with. While we have a duty to perform in the passing of suitable legislation, and in regard to the enforcement of that legislation, we also have a duty to perform in maintaining the right of free discussion in this country, and it is to be regretted that the experience we have had in dealing with the censorship which has been imposed has been along lines which certainly give reason for alarm to any person who values the right of free discussion or the common liberty of the subject, when it is proposed to put an enactment in these terms on the statute book.
My hon. friend the Minister of Justice insists that the words "or in any manner whatsoever to embarrass the Government
	/
or th$ minister in the administration of this Act or the regulations thereunder," do not apply to criticism of the Government or of the minister in the enforcing of the Act. Our experience with the censorship would certainly compel us to believe that criticism of the minister or the Government in regard to the administration of the Act would be interpreted as an embarrassment of the Government and the minister, and would render the individual liable to the penalties provided in this section. I am one of the old-fashioned people who believe in the right of free speech, who believe in the liberty of the subject, who believe that there cannot be good administration and good legislation without fair and reasonable criticism; and I say the attempt to impose such a provision as this on the country under the excuse of the existence of war conditions is a deliberate attempt to use those war conditions as a means of depriving the people of Canada of a very considerable share of that liberty for which their fathers fought, and for which our sons are fighting to-day.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
I would suggest that the word "wilfully" be inserted, making the paragraph read: "any person who wilfully by means of," etc. Supposing a lawyer were called upon for his opinion as to whether a man should report under the law and he advised that according to his reading of the law it was not necessary for this man to report, what would be the position? I think everybody would be protected if the word "wilfully" were added to the paragraph. I would also strike out the words which refer to a minimum penalty. It seems to me if they remain the result will be to defeat the purpose of the Act, because there may be cases where the contravention would be very trivial. It might be simply a remark, en passant, "I don't think you are bound-to report considering the conditions you are under." The judge will be in the presence of some very trivial offence, for which a most severe penalty is inflicted, and he may force his conscience, and say: "I will render a verdict of 'not guilty'." I am prepared to admit it is a grave offence, but we have a great number of offences provided for under the criminal laws in this country where the maximum penalty is fourteen years and there is no minimum- it is left entirely to the discretion of the judge. I would leave the question of a minimum penalty to the judge in this case. If there is a minimum penalty provided it may place the judge in a very awkward

position, and I endorse what my hon. friend from Cape Breton North (Mr. McKenzie) and my hon. friend from Prescott (Mr. Proulx) have said in this connection. I have seen cases of offences against the Post Office Act, for instance, where judges were very much embarrassed. The minimum penalty fixed was three yeaTS, but the judge and especially the juries-as my hon. friend the Minister of Justice well knows-would find the accused " not guilty," because the minimum penalty was too severe. If the Government has any confidence in the judges who will administer this law they Should be given a discretionary power to decide whether the penalty will be one hour imprisonment, or five years. I feel it my duty to tell the House, after an experience of twenty-two years before the criminal courts, that there are some offences against an Act which would be amply punished by one hour's imprisonment. I address my remarks particularly to the hon. Minister of Justice, and I know that from his fifteen years' experience on the Bench he would have done away with those minimum penalties if he bad had the power.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
We are dealing here with a criminal offence, and, of course, for any criminal offence there n ust be criminal intent. If is not a mere accidental interpretation of words that would render a man liable to conviction. I do not think there is any serious ground for apprehension that anybody will suffer undue consequence because of the omission of the word my hon. friend refers to.
As to the question of minimum penalty, laws are for prevention as well as for punishment, and I think that the nature of the offence that is contemplated here is *such that it is highly important to have the law produce in the fullest degree its preventive effect. For that purpose and in that view, it is well that it should be made perfectly clear to anybody who may be tempted to offend in this direction from the time that this law comes into force, that there will be grave consequences attached to his action. I can conceive of no circumstances under which one year's imprisonment would be too severe a penalty upon a man deservedly convicted of this offence. The class of men who will commit this offence will be a Class of men deserving, in my judgment, of condign punishment. If there should be exceptional cases such as have been referred to, the court would have the privilege of suspending sentence, and there is always the opportunity of exercising executive clemency, so that there will be a remedy for the exceptional cases referred to by the hon. gentleman; and I do not think that to prevent such possible exceptional cases the country should be deprived of the protection resulting from the general knowledge that those who seek, Without exposing themselves, to incite other people to unlawful resistance to the execution of this law, will, on conviction, suffer at least imprisonment for one year.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
If a judge, after
hearing a case, is embarrassed by finding the punishment too severe and reports to the executive, the Minister of Justice cannot advise the judge to impose a penalty of three months; he will have to tell the magistrate to let the law follow its course. As to suspending sentence, I have grave doubt as to the right of judges to suspend sentences, and this action on their part is often severely, and I think properly, criticised. As to executive clemency, the Department of Justice have simply the printed factums and depositions before them, and have not the same opportunity of judging the evidence as the magistrate who observes the witnesses in the box and can so determine whether they are entitled to credit. This offence would be a most grave, a most heinous one, according to circumstances; tout it -may be trivial too. Then why not leave it to the magistrate who has the discretion to raise it from one year to five, to exercise discretion in imposing a sentence from nothing up to five years.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
apprehends danger from oases where the magistrate will be of the opinion that this is too severe a sentence. In such a case the executive would be advised by the magistrate of his views, and it would be quite different from a case in which the executive would toe called upon to overrule the decision of the judge. I find it difficult to conceive of cases where a conviction would properly be made for this offence where a' year's imprisonment would be too severe punishment.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
I wish to emphasize
what has been said by the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver). I am a free British subject, and if there is one th'ng which I admire in British institutions, it is the freedom of the press and the freedom oE speech. I understand that my hon. friend assumes a share of responsibility for the drafting of this legislation.

I am surprised that he should claim the paternity of, and responsibility for framing, such drastic legislation. It is admitted that there is no parallel in Great Britain, or the United States, or even in Germany, for such a law. In none of these countries was similar legislation ever framed to give effect to a law passed by Parliament. Many of us have travelled in Great Britain, and if there is anything which struck me, as a Canadian of French blood, whenever I visited England, it was the great freedom of speech which existed in that country. The first time I went to London I was told by my friends not to fail to go to Hyde Park on Sunday morning, after service, and listen to the various speeches which were delivered there by agitators, socialists, parsons and political speakers, each of them claiming his right, as a free British subject, to criticise, as severely as possible, any legislation which to him appeared obsolete or drastic, and I am yet to be told that the British Government has ever taken any action against the speakers who, from time immemorial, condemned the Government at Hyde Park.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: In war time?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Yes. I will give a case in point. England is at war, and this evening's papers to-day will show my hon. friend that thousands of people are blaming the Government for not using reprisals against the air raids on London. This is embarrassing the Government, although we have the declaration of several of the ministers of the Crown that it is against the grain for Britishers to make reprisals of the German kind. I desire to give a case in point. I was speaking of the freedom any man has in England to combat legislation which has been enacted.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: To resist the operation?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Yes, and I will give my hon. friend a case in point at once. I was in England in 1906, and one of the largest meetings I ever witnessed was one held at the base of Nelson's monument in London. It was after the Balfour Government had passed the Education Act, and that Act was resisted by the various dissentients in England, and by the various sects, and I remember hearing a speech by the Rev. Dr. Clifford, asking the people to resist, by passive resistance the operation of that legislation. So much was that the case, that a few months afterwards, when Mr. Asquith came into office the legislation was repealed. I will

give another instance to the Minister of [DOT] Justice. An Act was passed by the British Parliament in 1914, the year of the war, and what happened? Sir Edward Carson went to Ulster. Did he flput the law? Did he put the law in defiance? Why he addressed the people of Ulster and preached resistance, and, to-day, that rebel is one of the ministers of the Crown. He used freedom of speech. He over-reached it, in my judgment, and in the judgment also of the Minister of Justice, and yet, to-day, in Great Britain, the man wh.o preached treason and rebellion in Ulster against an Act of His Majesty is the First Lord of the Admiralty. The Minister of Justice claims parentage for the very many amendments to this measure; I offer him my sincere compliments on those amendments, and I wish him success.
Mr. DO'HERTY:	The hon. gentleman
condemns the action of Sir Edward Carson, and then condemns me for framing legislation to prevent like action in this country. I ask how he connects the two things. The statement he has just made demonstrates that there ought to be a law in Canada to prevent people doing that kind of thing-taking his description of what Sir Edward Carson did. We have more respect in this country for law than the hon. gentleman represents that Sir Edward - Carson had. I am not proposing to be led into a discussion about matters with regard to which my opinions are absolutely well known, but if the hon. gentleman wanted to select an instance to justify legislation of this kind, he has given us instances, as he has described them, of open, flagrant, flouting of the law going uncontrolled. If his description be correct, all I can say is that there was a lack of firmness on the part of those charged with the enforcement of the law. I certainly will not sympathize-and I am quite satisfied that the House does not sympathize -with the advocacy of the doctrine that if we go throughout this wide world and find a place where anybody flouted laws and threatened resistance, such action should be held up to us for our admiration, and as an example for us to follow. I do not think the Ihon. gentleman has been very happy in the selection of the instance which he has cited.

speechtext: That is the hon. gentleman's view; that the man who criticises the Government is guilty under this Act. I had thought that the man who criticised the Government was in the exercise of his liberty, which this Act in no way embarrasses. This section lends itself so absolutely to no criticism that in order to make an argument, hon. gentlemen have to say that the section is something which it is not, and hence we have condemnation of laws which do things that this law does not pretend to do. I do not want to use too strong an expression; I shall simply say that no lawyer with any respect for his opinion would contend that this law pretends to say what hon. gentlemen have suggested. I am satisfied that any layman who will sit down and read it, not seeking to find what is not in it, would never dream of its talking about criticism of the minister or of the Government. It talks in very clear language of a variety of ways of hindering and impeding the operation of this Act and of a variety of ways of striving to induce people to hinder and impede and embarrass the operation of this Act. That is all it talks about.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: What is the meaning of the word " influences " in this section? Let me put a concrete case. Some member of this House, in rendering an account to hi3 electors of the position that he has taken may feel disposed to give his reasons for having criticised the compulsory service Bill and may be very strong in his denunciation of that Bill. Some persons in the audience may afterwards take exception to the way that he has spoken, saying that what he said had influenced a number of people to oppose the law. Thereupon they lay a complaint before two judges, who, for argument's sake, may be two tailors. Tailors are very respectable men, but they may not be learned in the law. These two tailors take up the word " influences " and they say: Yes, that member of Parliament certainly has influenced the electors, and, therefore, is guilty under this section of the law. I would like a pronouncement on thus subject. The Minister of Justice may be a little bit fatigued; perhaps the Solicitor General will answer.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Where do tailors come in in the matter of trying summary convictions?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: They might be justices of the peace.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Then there is an appeal.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: That is not answering.my question, I am putting a concrete case and I would like the Solicitor General to give me his opinion. It is a case that might readily arise. If a member of the House, having criticised the Government for bringing in this Conscription Bill, were charged before justices of the peace or your local tribunal, call it what you will, with having influenced his electors to resist conscription, would he, under such circumstances, be found guilty, or what latitude would be shown?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Clearly, he would be
tried for what he said, not for what he did or for what misinterpretations the electors may have put upon what he said. If he said something in itself influencing them to resist the law, he will be guilty. But the member of Parliament in question would not be guilty if he criticised this law, saying that he was opposed .to it, and contended that it should not have been passed.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: And gave his reasons.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
And gave his reasons
for being opposed to the law. So long as the member invites nobody to resist it; so long as nothing is Intended to influence any one to resist the law, the fact that a man goes away from the meeting and proceeds to resist the law would not, I am sure, result in the conviction of the member by any court of average intelligence, upon the ground not of what he said or did, but of the mental operations of some of the people who heard him. I think we can trust the courts to interpret the case in that way.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Following that up, we shall see that the next day the city papers, if the case occurs in a city, report what that man has said, and misreport his words. The minister will agree with me that that is very often done. Would the newspaper be considered to be guilty of a crime as having influenced people through the publication of a misreported speech?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
If the newspaper mis-reports the speech, that is to say, if it does not reproduce what was said, then that newspaper will have to take the responsibility for what it sends out to the public,

if it sends out matter of a nature to influence men to resist the law.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: It is the newspapers we shall have to get after.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: The newspapers will not have any greater liberty to seek to inspire resistance .to this law than the individual who does not own a newspaper will have.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Of course, I may be pressing these details, but this is the first time, in my existence at least, that in this country I have been up against any, law which would tend to limit the right of speech or the liberty of the press. It would be well for the minister to go just as far as he possibly can in giving detailed cases of what latitude will be allowed to men to speak-for instance, members of Parliament or political candidates to their electors, or any citizens, and how far newspapers may go. Because, while I may have implicit confidence in tribunals, I have not always the greatest confidence in the World in Justices of the Peace, although they may be well meaning.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I think my hon. friend will see that there is an almost infinite vafiety of ways iri which this section might be contravened, and that it would be absolutely impossible, and more than that a highly unprofitable task, to attempt to enumerate them here this evening.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
The Prime Minister has certainly put the case in a nutshell. There is an absolutely infinite variety of instances in which the terms of this section might be contravened, and the citizen left liable to serious punishment. We do not object to reasonable legislation to secure the enforcement of and respect for any law, but we do object to the use of indefinite and comprehensive terms by the use of which innocent parties are made subject to severe penalties. That is the meaning that I am compelled to take out of the reading of this section. The minister has seen fit to read it in his own way. The way that I read it is this:
Any person who, by means of any written or oral communication or by any public speech or utterance, or in any manner whatsoever, takes such action as will embarrass the Government or the minister in the administration of this Act or the regulations thereunder, shall be guilty of an offence.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: In that, the hon. member is entirely mistaken.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Not ten minutes ago, I heard the minister announce to the House that this was to be used as a threat. Its importance was in its preventive capability as much as in its punitive capability. Then, the minister surely must have used a form of words covering the possibility of severe punishment, or	there would be no
threat in it. When the power is placed in the hands of any authority, the tendency is to use, or even to misuse that power, and the more extensive the power, the greater the liability to misuse it. I am going to contend that such a law intended to terrorize the public from the
10 p.m. use of free speech and from the employment of just criticism of matters of administration in which the people are concerned is not a law that tends to the well-being of the country. On July 4, 1917, Lord Northcliffe, speaking to the National Press Club at Washington on the subject of censorship said:
The danger of a censorship is that it may be used to exalt incompetence to impair efficiency by hiding mismanagement, to weaken resolution by exaggerated optimism. The dangers of misuse of the power of censorship are well known to those who know what we suffered from the hiding of the truth about the war for the first two years.
That is merely in regard to the censorship of the press, but this is a section involving the censorship of the people, the censorship of the right of free speech. I will not delay the House; I have placed

my opinions before it as clearly and as definitely as I am able to do, and I will only take the liberty of reading from the Orange Sentinel of the 12th of July-
' An hon. MEMBER: Glorious day.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
-just exactly what appears to my mind to be the import of this particular enactment. The Sentinel says:
The glorious revolution of 1688 put an end In Great Britain and throughout the British Empire to the doctrine that Kings rule by Divine Right.
Now all we have to do is to change the word "Kings" to "Governments," and we are not to forget that we have to-day a Government that is putting into force a Conscription Act upon a disfranchised people. The Sentinel goes on to say:
The Kaiser, posing as the annointed of Almighty God, is sending his people to the slaughter by the hundred thousand. He claims it to be his Divine right to do so. He denies to his people any real share in the government of the country, in the declaration of war, and in the continuance of the struggle. He is an autocrat after the pattern of James II. That monarch claimed the right by Divine appointment to suspend the laws of the country. He aimed not only to suspend the civil laws but the religious laws.
Further on, this article says:
When William and Mary took the crown from Parliament, they acknowledged the supremacy of the people, and thus founded the first great democratic state among the modern nations. Upon the foundation laid by William of Orange rests the present superstructure of the British Empire.
And the Government of to-day, ruling by Divine right, undertakes to deprive Canada of the right of free speech which was guaranteed to it by the revolution which placed William of Orange otn the Throne.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: The Minister of Justice was reading the law to me a moment ago. subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.

There are many laws which provide for the suspension of habeas corpus. I do not know whether gov-

ernments that govern by diabolical right are more to his taste or not.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: By democratic right.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.

speechtext: That is not applicable to citizens of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I do not think that the principle varies so much.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I think it varies a great deal.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Will the minister not agree to the suggestion that this clause be revised so as to actually convey, even to such a mind as mine, the intent the minister declares it to convey?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
I speak with all respect, but I do not know any words in the English language that will make it clearer; it must be my limitation, of course, but I must avow my limitation. If the hon. gentleman sees in these words power to punish people for criticising the Government, then I do not know any words in the English or any other language that I could possibly use that would not convey to the hon. gentleman the meaning that people are to be imprisoned for criticising the Government. I do not know how I could alter it. I have left all that kind of thing entirely out. What more can I do? In all frankness, if the hon. gentleman will tell me what words I could use that would not convey the meaning to him that I make it an offence to criticise the Government, and that will convey the meaning that I want to convey as clearly and emphatically as I can, that those will be punished who encourage people to impede or hinder the operations of this law or to induce pr persuade people to embarrass the Government or the minister in its operation-if there is any other form that I can use that will convince the hon.

gentleman that I am not making a law to punish criticism of the Government, I will be glad to consider it. I have tried not to say that, and I have not said it, but still the hon. gentleman reads that into the section and says, " Now, won't you reconsider the section and read that out of it?"

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: As the minister has appealed to me I think the situation would 'be relieved if he were to strike out the words " in any manner whatsoever to embarrass the Government or the minister in the administration of this Act or the regulations thereunder."

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman
will read the section I think he will see that it is not made an offence to embarrass the Government or the Minister of Justice in the administration of this Act or the regulations thereunder; that is not what is made the offence. The verb " embarrass " is in the infinitive mood; it is "to embarrass," which necessarily means that it follows on something else. What is made the offence is this: the offence is the inducing or influencing people to do all these things that follow. After making it an offence to impede or hinder, and so on, the section goes on:
-or persuades, induces or influences, or attempts to persuade, induce or influence any person or any body or class of persons.
to do a number of things, the last of those things being " to embarrass the Government." The offence is the persuading or inducing or influencing or attempting to persuade, induce or influence any person to do any of these things, or the persuading or endeavouring to get people to embarrass the Government.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Why not leave it
to-the general law? Section 69 of the Criminal Code, to which the minister referred, should cover this.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
The sections to which
I referred have to do with a number of different kinds of offences. The analogy is this. These sections .make it an offence to incite people to commit that particular kind of crime. Here we have made a new law; we are imposing new obligations, and [DOT]we are putting into this Act a provision in substance that inciting any one to a violation of this Act shall be an offence. The Criminal Code says it shall be an offence to bill a man or to incite somebody else to kill a mian. We say: Certain things must be done under this Act, and it shall be an offence for anybody to incite anybody else to contravention of this Act. That is following out what is almost the general rule. It is perhaps open to the argument that possibly we might find general provisions which would meet the case. But is it not fair to the public, if it is true, to put them on their guard in this Act, that interference with the Act is an offence? I do not pretend to carry the whole Criminal Code in my mind, but I am strongly of the opinion there is a general provision with regard to obstructing the operation of law, and if there is no special provision, then at common law it would be an offence. But we want to provide appropriate penalties for the incitement to violation of this law or the obstruction of its operation, and we do think-notwithstanding what the hon. member from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) said about this being a threat-it is important that we should have the full preventive effect that may result from calling the attention of those who may be tempted to offend in that manner to the fact that it is an offence carrying serious punishment. In the second place, I think there is in this an element of fairness to those who may be tempted to offend in this regard. Any one who reads the newspapers is quite aware that there are persons who have been boasting of their intention to hinder the operation of this law, and asserting how easy it will be for them to make it entirely inoperative. I do not wish to refer to previous debates in this House, but I think one could make citations from some speeches in which we were told how absolutely inoperative this law was going to be, and what an arsenal of weapons was in the hands of people to prevent this law from becoming effective.. I think people should have their attention called to the gravity of such statements, and perhaps it is only fair to bring it home to them now, that when they start doing it they are committing a grave offence, and will be liable to grave punishment.
v Mr. OLIVER: If I followed the argument of my hon. friend, this section applies to the man who incites, but does not apply to the man who personally embarrasses the Government or the minister. Is that the understanding?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
As regards the particular matter of embarrassing the Government or the Administration in carrying out the law, so far as "embarrassment" is concerned, it has a different meaning from "hinder" or "impede." Embarrassment of the Government is not in itself made a specific

offence. What is made an offence is for people to embarrass the Government in the operation of this law. The provision is not intended to deal with people coming under the direct operation of this law and who disobey it. They are dealt with under other sections of the Act. The people we are trying to reach here are those who set to work to hinder or impede the application of this law by their own actions or conduct, and those who seek to persuade others to hinder or to impede the application of the law. With regard to the offence of seeking to persuade, we have included those who seek to persuade others to embarrass the Government or the minister in the administration of this Act, though we have not taken the act of embarrassing the Government or the minister as constituting an offence in itself. What is sought to be reached, and what I think this House would agree with me ought to be reached, is a class of people who either because they do not come under the Act or because they have not the courage to take any risks themselves, want to stand behind, and through newspapers or by speeches or by any other method, try to rouse up other people-perhaps unthinking people who do not quite understand- and get them into a frame of mind where they will proceed to try to hamper and embarrass the administration of this Act. 1 should think everybody ought to be agreed that this class of persons should foe punished. I can understand there may be a large measure of sympathy with those who are subject to the application of the principal provisions of the Act, and who may be tempted not to submit willingly to its operation, but I cannot understand extending sympathy to or seeking to shield the man who, not coming under the Act himself and therefore taking no risks, seeks to lead other people into committing either a direct violation of the Act or to hinder or impede the operation of the Act or to embarrass the Government in trying to carry it out. A man of that class should have no sympathy from any one.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
I quite understand that any man who incites others to resist the law or to disobey the law comes under the provisions of the Criminal Code, and I have no sympathy with such a man. But does not my hon. friend see that this clause deals with a political measure? Conscription is a political measure, passed by a moribund Parliament. By the very nature of things it will be the issue before the

people of Canada at the next election. I say to my hon. friend, in all sincerity, that by enacting this drastic condition he is simply sowing the seed for informers in this country. What will happen? Say a meeting is held in nay hon. friend's constituency in Montreal. His political opponent, surrounded by sympathizers and political speakers, will criticise the Government or will criticise my hon. friend, not only for having enacted this measure when Parliament was functus officio, but for all the shortcomings and failings of the Govefnment during the last six years. There will be informers -at that meeting, and these informers will report the castigations inflicted on my hon. friend or on the Government by the speakers.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
It is not an offence to
castigate me. In any event, I may say they do not do it in my constituency.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
These informers will
report the castigations, and an information will be laid. My hon. friend knows the political gaime will be played in his electoral division.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: By you.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
The animus is tnere.
An information will be laid against the speaker, and he will appear before the court. He may be found guilty according to the evidence brought by the informers. So far so good. The judgment or verdict of the court is there, he is sentenced. It is a political question arising out of a political meeting between political opponents, and yet the man whose words have been -misconstrued and distorted will not have the privilege of invoking the Habeas Corpus Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
My hon. friend is under a misapprehension. There is nothing in this Act to deprive a man of a writ of habeas corpus. This would not be a proceeding before a tribunal, and therefore would not be affected by the section under consideration. Such a man would be brought before the ordinary civil courts and he would have all the rights and privileges enjoyed by any other person who is brought before the courts of the country for any offence. What is sought by this subsection is to avoid having the operation of the tribunals interfered with and retarded by having the tribunals brought before the judges of the courts on injunction, certiorari, mandamus or some other proceeding. I read in the paper the other day the speech of a lawyer, whom I respect

both as a lawyer and a gentleman, who said that this Act would never operate because they would take all cases to the civil courts and keep them there until the war was over. My friend's friend who is coming down to castigate me can castigate to his heart's content, and when he has done castigating, if I have anything to say about it, it will not be in the way of prosecuting him; I will take care of my defence in that matter. But if anybody wishes to prosecute him for that castigation he will take him before the ordinary courts and nothing in this Act will affect any remedy, right or recourse that he will have under the general law ot the country.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: He may be taken before the courts, but he will not have the remedies of the law, he will not .have the writ of habeas corpus or the injunction.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: But the case put by the hon. member for Rouville is not one that would ever come before any of the tribunals. It is not provided that a man who is prosecuted for violating the Act will be prosecuted anywhere except before the ordinary courts, and there he will have all the usual remedies. The only thing that the tribunals provided for under this Act can deal with or decide is the question whether or not a man shall be granted a certificate of exemption from military service; and it is intended that that shall be decided by these tribunals provided for in this Act without interference from any other court.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: So that the offence under subsection 2 is of a different nature from that under subsection 3?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: There is no question of offence in subsection 3.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Subsection 3 has nothing to do with offences.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: As regards subsection 2, we have all the remedies that the law provides.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: It creates an offence for which a man is liable to be indicted or convicted on summary proceedings.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: In other words, if anybody is indicted under the general law, lie has all the remedies of the law; but if anybody is prosecuted under this Act, he is deprived of all the remedies of the law.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: No.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
How can it be
otherwise?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Subsection 2 creates a certain offence and says it is punishable on indictment, that is before the ordinary criminal court.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I understand all that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Subsection 3 provides:
No proceeding authorized or pending before any of the tribunals provided for by this Act and no decision of any such tribunal shall by means of injunction, prohibition, mandamus, certiorari, habeas corpus or other process whether of the like kind or otherwise issuing out of any court be enjoined, restrained, stayed, removed or subjected to review or consideration upon any ground whether arising out of alleged absence of jurisdiction in the tribunal, nullity, defect or irregularity of the proceedings or any other cause whatsoever nor shall any such proceeding or decision be questioned, reviewed or reconsidered collaterally in any action or proceeding, civil or criminal.
Now, the general court before, which a man is indicted is not the tribunal provided by this Act, it is a tribunal existing irrespective of this Act, and will exist after this Act has ceased to have any effect. The tribunals provided for by this Act are the local tribunal, the appeal tribunal and the Central Appeal Judge. Proceedings before those three tribunals under this Act cannot be removed into any other court by any process whatever, to be reconsidered there. That is the entire effect of this.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
I understand that. If I impede the Government, and
. embarrass them in every possible way, I am not liable to indictment, under section 2.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is liable.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
If I say to Mr. Wilson, "Now you embarrass the Government,'' and if he is foolish enough to follow my example, I become liable to prosecution, but if I do the act myself, I am not liable. I may be liable otherwise, but not under this section. The man who induces the other to act is liable, but the man who takes the action is not liable. Then section 3 deals with another class of offence altogether. We pass to the prosecution of the offences which are created by this Act. The young man who goes before the first tribunal, and appeals, and so on, is dealt with by those tribunals, and is deprived of all the remedies of the law. That is what the section means. Why should this man be deprived of all the remedies provided by the law? Why should he not be accorded the privileges of British subjects, when all

these provisions are framed for the protection of the freedom and liberty of the subject?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: It is not a question of offences under this section at all. It is a question of a decision as to whether a man should have a certificate, or whether he should be refused a certificate, and these tribunals will be established for the purpose of determining that question. It is intended that they should have exclusive jurisdiction to deal with it, and, for the purpose of protecting that exclusive jurisdiction for the determination of that question, interference by other courts is prohibited, and the reason of the enumeration of the different processes by which other courts might interfere in cases in which they are entitled to interfere is simply so that we might make it quite clear that, by no means whatever is any other court to interfere. The effect of this provision is simply to establish that the jurisdiction for the determination of these oases shall belong exclusively to this court.	>

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: That is what I complain of.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
If that is what is complained of, that would not apply to the case the hon. gentleman refers to. The matter to be determined requires to be promptly determined, and we cannot wait till the war is over for a decision. The questions, in their nature, are, in the great bulk of cases at all events, questions proper to be determined by a jury, in any ordinary court. More than that, we have -taken care to submit the decisions of -all of these tribunals to the judges of the ordinary civil courts of the country, in the way specified in this Act, so that we extend to the individual the protection, not only of the judge of first instance, but of a judge of the Supreme Court, to see that this is done rightly. Having given him all of tliese protections, all that is sought to be done by this provision is to prevent his seeking to have an appeal to other courts, to get them to determine a matter over which to-day they have absolutely no jurisdiction, and, unless this Act gave it to them, could have no jurisdiction. But abuses of the processes of the law happen repeatedly, and if this section be not enacted people, under pretext of lack of jurisdiction, or unconstitutionality, or -anything whatsoever, no matter how unfounded may seek -to go to some other court or courts, not because they have a right to, but by misrepresenting the situation, and 
once they get launched before those other courts you would have these interminable appeals.
We have -sought to make provisions to enable these -tribunals, in a proper way, to carry out this section practically, effectively and within a reasonable time, and to throw round them the protection of the judiciary of this country in this way; and having done that, we say now we shall make it absolutely impossible for anybody acting in bad faith to seek to remove this -question from the tribunals appointed to deal with it, and by means of processes of different kinds, to spin out the litigation in regard to it until the war is over. That is what we have to guard against, and this is not at all unusual. Wherever, with regard to a. particular question, exclusive jurisdiction is given to a particular court, that ends the remedy in any other court.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: When the application is reached, it can be thrown out if it is frivolous. But my bon. friend here seeks to deprive the British subjects of remedies which have always been sacred to them. Legislation prohibiting the exercise of rights and prerogatives is always looked upon with extreme disfavour.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
The provisions of
subsections 2 and 5 of this section aTe extreme and unusual, interfering with the right of free speech and of free discussion in the press. These proposed provisions, therefore, are worthy of the closest attention of the committee. The Minister of Justice has indicated the class of people whom he desires to reach through subsection 2. I submit that the cases to which he refers are sufficiently provided for by the first subsection. My hon. friend goes far beyond hiis stated purpo.se when he makes it an offence for a .person to do anything which will induce any one to embarrass the Government or the minister in the administration of this Act. He says that this section is to come into force when the Act
receives the assent of His Excellency and before the Military Service Bill goes into operation. It is constituting an offence that nobody ever heard of to go- before a justice of the peace and say that during the course of .a political discussion some one used words which were calculated to induce some one else to do something that would embarrass the Government in carrying out the terms of an Act which was not in existence. If you have a court which is willing to receive information of that kind, what matter of proof would be submitted to it in order to get a conviction? My hon. friend is going too far when he leaves it to a gentleman not learned in the law who may happen to be a justice of the peace to say whether a man who criticised the Government, as be had a perfect right to do, during the course of a political discussion which he had a perfect right to engage in, was embarrassing the Government in the operation of an ,Aet that was not in existence. If the justice of the peace was a keen supporter of my hon. friend-and some of these justices of the peace are-you can fancy what sort of evidence he would require in order to satisfy him that the Government was being embarrassed. I think that we ought to have a definition of what the word "embarrass" means. What does my hon. friend mean by embarrassing the Government?' The word is capable of definition; the phraseology should not be left in such general form, to be interpreted at will by ' any justice of the peace in the country. The right to criticise this Government is a right that should be preserved if the democracy which is at stake in this war is to be upheld in Canada. My hon. friend is going too far if he seeks to take away the right of legitimate criticism of those who are entrusted with the conduct of public affairs in this country. My hon. friend will say: You can appeal from the decision of the justice of the peace in this regard. But consider the humiliation of a perfectly honest man who, with no desire to do anything improper, is convicted by a justice of the peace under this provision. That man has certain views which he has a right to express, either in writing or verbally, to those who are willing to attend to him. First, then, there should be a definition of the word "embarrass;" secondly, the right of legitimate and honest criticism on the part of the free citizens of this country should be preserved.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

Embarrassing the Government or the minister in the administration or operation of this Act is the equivalent of creating difficulties or of placing difficulties in the way of putting the Act into operation.

He is asking it to interpret language which is specially technical. I am dealing with the period that exists between the coming into force of this section after His Excellency sanctions the Act, and the time when the Military Service Act is declared to be in force. Too much power, is put into the hands of a justice of the peace if you enable him, at the instance of any informer, to ruin the good name of any man so that he would have to go to a higher court to get rid of the stigma attached to his name. Why should not the minister preserve the reasonable right of criticism to a decent citizen of the country who does not pretend to take the position of that class of men which the minister says is the class he intends to go after?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.

and an extraordinary law. If the minister would agree to insert a provision that no proceedings should be taken under this Act except with the consent of himself or his department, that would relieve the minds of the people very materially.

speechtext:
I hope the Minister of Justice will accept the suggestion of my hon. friend from North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie), and that it will be made clear that citizens of this country will not be deprived of their Tight of criticising even this Act or any other piece of legislation of this Government. According to subsection 6:
This section shall come into force on. the day of the sanction of this Act.
The Prime Minister, when he appealed to my right hon. leader to form a coalition Government, stated that this law would be passed and then an appeal to the country would follow. In addition to that the Prime Minister, when introducing this Bill, said that he was considering the advisability of submitting this law to the people of Canada before enforcing it. Further than that, the constitution of this country prescribed that there shall be an election in a few months. Evidently the issue at this election will be this very law of conscription. It was, I believe, in the mind of the Prime Minister when he made his offer to the leader of the Opposition to appeal to the country for the purpose of submitting this law. If the issue is conscription, is it fair to put into force subsection 6, and thus make it an offence for any one to criticise this measure? I am sure the Government, in appealing to the country on this issue, does not intend to prevent the opponents of the Bill from presenting their case to their electors. When the Conscription Bill was introduced in the British House of Commons, somebody stated that to apply the Bill to Ireland would be a national crime and a folly. I believe myself that imposing conscription on Canada is a folly and a crime, and I intend to say so to my eleo-tors.

not see how it can be considered, as coming under the provisions of this section. speechtext: Is it the understanding of the law that it will be no part of the responsibility of the Minister of Justice or of the Government to prosecute the man who does not answer the call of his class?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
I was dealing, and I understood the hon. gentleman to be dealing, with the question of the punishment of people who seek to hinder the execution of this law. I pointed out that it would not be necessary for the Minister of Justice to intervene in order that there should be a prosecution unless I accepted the suggestion of my hon. friend from Cape Breton. If I did not do so, I could not intervene to prevent the supposed constituents of the Minister of Inland Revenue from being pros-

eeuted if anybody wanted to prosecute him. I cannot see how from what I have said the inference has been drawn that I would not be interested in seeing the law enforced. I have already pointed out that I would be neither hindered nor embarrassed if the Minister of Inland Revenue should call upon me under those circumstances. In the first place I do not think he would ask me to refrain from action in any circumstances where it was my duty to act, but if I did accept the hypothesis of my hon. friend, I do not think it would make any difference to my action in the matter.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
The provisions of clause 2 are not aimed at persons who use thoughtless words. They are not aimed at all at ,criticism. It is one thing to criticise those responsible for the enactment of a law; it is another thing to incite people to refuse to obey that law after it has properly passed.
The two things are absolutely distinct and apart. This clause does not touch the first case at all; it is designed most distinctly to touch the second. But even so, it is not designed to prosecute every person who may utter some thoughtless word. It is designed to prevent a serious attempt to reduce this law to a mere nullity; that is its purpose, and that purpose, I think, ought to commend itself to the judgment of every member in this House and every man in the country, because when the people fail in their respect for a law which has been properly passed a condition will have been reached which will not augur well for the future of the country.
The suggestion of my hon. friend from North Cape Breton is quite in line with the purpose for which this section has been proposed. If he will be good enough to let the Bill pass, with the understanding that we will take his suggestion into consideration,
I shall be obliged, and if it is desired to revert to the matter again in case we should not accept his suggestion we shall be very glad to do so.

No proceeding authorized or pending before any of the tribunals provided for by this Act and no decision of any such tribunal shall by means of injunction, prohibition, mandamus, certiorari, habeas corpus or other process whether of the like kind or otherwise issuing out of any court be enjoined, restrained, stayed, removed or subjected to review or consideration upon any ground whether arising

out of alleged absence of jurisdiction in the tribunal, nullity, defect or irregularity of the proceedings or any other cause whatsoever nor shall any such proceeding or decision be questioned, reviewed or reconsidered collaterally in any action or proceeding, civil or criminal.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
This clause has been fully explained by the Minister of Justice. As he has pointed out, it is not designed to deal with cases of prosecution for offences. It is merely designed, like a great many similar enactments, to prevent interference on technical grounds with the operations of the tribunals. Innumerable	sections of	this	kind	are tobe found in legislation in this country ;	they are to	be	found	in	the
Canada Temperance Act, in the enactments of provincial legislatures with regard to liquor, in the Immigration Act, and in many other Acts which one could enumerate if it were necessary. The object is a very clear one. The enforcement of laws of this character is very often confided to persons who are not thoroughly versed in the law, and are therefore liable to make mistakes of which advantage might be taken by application to a higher court. It is the purpose of these enactments that technical objections of that character shall not be available to those who seek to defeat the law; that is clarly the purpose of section 3, as it has been drafted and as it is now proposed

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: The object is well known. There are, however, precedents of this character, and they should not be considered as precedents. I think it is very dangerous legislation.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I would suggest that this clause is in the wrong place. The connection is bad, and it is very apt to be misleading. If this clause were at the end of clause 5 there would not be so much danger of misunderstanding.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.

On subsection 4 of proposed new section 16:
Nothing in this Act contained shall be held to mitigate or affect the punishment provided by any other Act or law lor the offence of assisting the enemy; nor shall anything in this Act, be held to limit or affect the powers of the Governor in Council under the War Measures Act, 1914.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: What is the meaning of this?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
There are matters dealt with in this Act-for instance, the matters we were speaking of a moment ago-that might be considered, according to the circumstances, as amounting to giving assistance to the enemy. There might be such hindrance of the operation of this Act as might be assisting the enemy. It is not intended by reason of the provisions here made to prevent the application of existing laws in regard to assistance of the enemy. We do not want to reduce the responsibility of any man for actions that may possibly be covered by this section, if the conditions and circumstances make them such as to amount to assisting the enemy; we do not want to withdraw such a man from the operation of the general laws upon that subject.
I am not prepared to point out particular cases where it does, but I think it is so highly probable that you might find cases of actually assisting the enemy which might come under the letter of this provision, that it is wise to make it clear that it is not intended by enacting this provision with regard to the operation of this Act to mitigate the law wherever it may be applicable with regard to assistance to the enemy.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Is there anything in this law so far which may be of any assistance to the enemy?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: This law is intended to hinder and impede the enemy. A man might carry on his operations for the purpose of hindering this law, and might so conduct himself for that purpose as to assist the enemy in effect and bring himself within other provisions dealing directly with assisting the enemy.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: For which a more serious punishment is provided.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.

Of course if it belonged to the Minister of Justice to order prosecutions under this Act, it would be for him to determine upon the facts of a case whether it constitutes a violation of some other law with regard to assisting the enemy for which the punishment may be heavier than this, and whether he should proceed under that other law, or whether the case merely came under this law. If it
is open to any one to lay an information without authorization from the Minister of Justice, it will be for the person laying the information to make up his mind what he wants to charge the party accused with. If he thinks he has a charge against him under this Act, he will proceed under this Act. If he thinks he has a charge involving more severe punishment under another law, he will proceed under another law.

Nobody will be tried before the local tribunals for an offence. Persons charged with those offences will be brought before the criminal courts. The local tribunal has power to decide only one question, and that is, is a particular man entitled to an exemption certificate.

(5) Any person who prints or publishes or causes to be printed or published in any book, newspaper, periodical, tract, pamphlet, circular or printed publication whatsoever any editorial, article, letter, correspondence or other matter intended or having effect to advocate, advise, persuade, instigate or influence the public or any person, body or class of persons to resist, obstruct, hinder or impede the due execution of this Act or compliance therewith in any respect or particular according to its true intent, meaning and purpose or for the purpose of impeding or defeating the operation or administration of this Act to abstain from submitting for decision of the proper tribunals claims for exemption or the evidence available in support thereof or in any manner whatsoever to embarrass the Government or the minister in the administration of this Act or the regulations thereunder shall be guilty of an offence and shall be liable upon indictment or upon summary conviction to imprisonment for a term not less than one year nor more than five years; and whether the printer or publisher of any such book, newspaper, periodical, tract, pamphlet, circular or printed publication shall have been first convicted or not the same shall be summarily suppressed and shall remain suppressed for the duration of the present war; and moreover the further publication of any book, newspaper, periodical, tract, pamphlet, circular or printed publication whatsoever in any issue of which any such editorial, article, letter, correspondence or other matter shall have been published is prohibited and the same shall be summarily suppressed and remain suppressed for the duration of the present war.

speechtext:
What does that mean?
What effect does it have on the prosecution of the case? It says whether the man responsible for the printing or publishing of the article be convicted or not the newspaper will toe suppressed. Does that involve the suppression of the newspaper even if the man were acquitted?
