speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: As far as the offence constituted here is concerned, it is precisely the same as the offence dealt with in subsection 2, except that this deals with the printing and publishing of it. If the party were acquitted, he might be acquitted because he was not the man who published it. Still, the publication is there to speak for itself, and if on its face it comes under this seotjon, then that publication, ought to be suppressed. Perhaps it was not the fault of the owner, and perhaps he is not responsible for what happened, but you must have the power of suppression even though you may not be able to find out who is the person responsible for the publication. The man who did it may not be convicted and punished, but the publication tending to hinder the operation of the Act is there-it is a substantial thing-it is not a question to go to the law courts about. We may not be able to find the man who published it, and the publisher of a particular paper may be able upon his prosecution to establish that the article slipped in unawares, but we do not want it to remain in circulation simply because it is not possible to convict somebody of having produced it. I think in. the majority of cases, where it was called for, there would be no difficulty in convicting the publisher; still the two things are provided for-the possible conviction of the publisher and the suppression of the paper, and it is pointed out that it is not essential for the one to be done that the other should be successful.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I can see that clearly; but suppose this were the case: that the proprietor who may be his own editor goes away temporarily and in good faith installs somebody else as editor in his absence. It very often occurs that the temporary man may publish something diametrically opposed to the policy of th8 paper and to the wishes of the proprietor. Does not the hon. minister think it a hardship that the owner, who is entirely innocent, and who has been taken advantage of, is to be robbed of his property by this Act. His paper is suppressed until the end of the war.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: What my hon. friend means is that under the provisions of this section the suppression would be obligatory; that we would be obliged to suppress it, because we use the wsrd "shall?"

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: It looks like that to me.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: There is some force in that. We might substitute the word " may."

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: An editor accused of being responsible for the publication of matter which is an infringement of this section has an opportunity on his teial of giving evidence in his own behalf and of being represented by counsel. Should not the proprietors of a newspaper have a similar right to be heard before their paper is suppressed?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
The section merely
makes provision that suppression may follow. It would be necessary to make provision by regulation for the steps which would lead to suppression. The power of suppression under the censorship regulations for the publication of seditious matter is exercised on the responsibility of the Government through the Department of the Secretary of State. It is a power that can only be exercised effectively by somebody acting in an executive capacity. If you have to go to the courts, the publication continues in the meantime and may render nugatory the purpose of the suppression.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Surely the men who have their money invested in a newspaper enterprise ought to have the right in the protection of their interests and property of having the question whether the article is an infraction of the Jaw tried out in exactly the same way as the accused man would be tried. That would seem to be elementary.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: It would, of course, be highly desirable to have the matter tried out before any suppression was made, but I do not see how that could be done effectively. Suppression is a power that is only effective if it is susceptible of prompt exercise. It would expose people to serious damage in their property if that power were unwisely exercised, but I do not see how it could be effectively exercised by the ordinary process of law. It goes without saying that the power of suppression would not be exercised by any minister without very grave consideration or on any but the clearest justification.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Who will have power to suppress a paper pending trial?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: The particular minister will have to be designated by regulation. In a general way the censorship is in the Department of State.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Is that not against the
principles of British justice that no man shall be declared guilty until he is found

guilty? You suppress the paper although the court has not declared whether there is anything in it which calls for suppression.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: If that be the case, and the court is not supposed to determine whether the newspapers should be suppressed or not, how can a judge be supposed to condemn the man who printed the article?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Those are two distinct things. The prosecution is one thing and the suppression of a newspaper.
either altogether or during the war, is another thing. In the course of this war, we have to deal with all the publications, for example, that come into the country. A number have been prevented from coming in because they were distinctly seditious. I think, in one case, a newspaper published in this country was suppressed for a certain length of time. These are not matters which could very well be delermined by the adjudication of a court. Any government that is conscious of its responsibility will exercise such powers most sparingly. I may take the committee into my confidence to the extent of saying that many communications have been sent to the Government from different parts of the country with regard to newspapers which, perhaps, were publishing matter of a detrimental character, but we have always felt, when such matters were brought to our attention, that it was only in a rather extreme case that the Government should exercise such extreme powers, and it is with a strong sense of responsibility that this Government, or any government, would take into consideration any such question.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
The .proposition to
suppress the paper first and try the editor afterwards reminds one of the policy adopted by Cardinal Richelieu, where the man was executed first and tried afterwards.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: We were obliged to deal in that way with a number of seditious publications that were coming into this country. There was no other way of dealing with them.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
The Prime Minister has suggested that the word " may " be used instead of the word " shall "-"This publication so found guilty shall be suppressed to the end of the war." I am not speaking from the standpoint of sympathy for the man responsible for the publication, but I may say that in every locality a weekly paper particularly is an institution. In punishing the guilty, you may be robbing a locality of an institution, which would mean a great deprivation to the people of that locality. Woulditnotbe wise foT the Government to take, by this Bill, powers of discretion to say whether the paper shall be suppressed till after the war, or for a period? For this reason: there might be some man who would take that paper who would perhaps assist very much in the prosecution of the war by his articles, and if the paper were suppressed, it could not be conducted at all thereafter. I make this suggestion

because if you rob some of the localities of their weekly paper, you might almost as well take their prayer books from them. I know the objection which might be made would be that the paper might be transferred to some person else, but really remain the property of the same individual. But if a bona fide sale were made, and the paper were conducted properly under the new management, it would save the locality from being deprived of what is an institution in a great many sections and a great benefit to the people.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: It might be suspended for a period not exceeding the duration of the war.	.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
As a mere layman, who has listened to lawyers for four hours, I will make a suggestion before this section is adopted. Most of us will be called upon to try and explain the meaning of the clauses to people who are not perhaps as familiar with these matters as we in this House are. Would it not be possible to paragraph these sections in such a way that the meaning would be a little bit clearer? For instance, that subsection 5, which we have been dealing with, and make it read something like this:
5. Any person who prints or publishes or causes to be printed or published in any book, newspaper, etc.,
(a)	or influence the public or any person, body or class of persons to resist, etc.,
(b)	or for the purpose of impeding or defeating the operation or administration of this Act to abstain from submitting for decision of the proper tribunal claims for exemption of the evidence available, etc.,
(c)	or in any manner whatsoever to embarrass the Government or the minister in the administration of this Act, etc.
If they were placed in that form, we should be able to see them, one after the other, and we poor laymen, who have not had the benefit of a legal education, might be able to explain it to our friends so that it would be understood.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I hope the hon. gentleman will be more successful than I was in getting the minister to break the section up into paragraphs. I tried to get it divided into sentences.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: We will make an effort to get back to our A. B. C.'s, and perhaps we will reach the comprehension of everybody.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
In regard to the question of the proprietor of a newspaper and the newspaper itself, we have always had the

understanding that the manager or the proprietor, when accused, would be brought up for trial, and would be tried on the merits of the question as to the offence committed through the publication of the article. Am I to understand, however, the Prime Minister has said that the trial of the man is only a question of establishing his identity or responsibility, but the question as to the nature of the article is a matter entirely for the Government through its censorship? If so, it is an arbitrary authority to be exercised by the Government; it is not to be a matter for the consideration of the court which tries the owner or manager of the paper.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I think my hon. friend must ibe referring to something that was said by the Minister of Justice; I do not remember touching upon the part of the question that he first mentioned. I pointed out that in these cases of censorship in respect of something that is regarded as detrimental to the public interest, the executive must exercise a certain responsibility, and that that responsibility, by reason of its character, must be, and had been up to the present time, exercised sparingly. The Government has possessed full powers to deal with this subject, and the cognate subject defined in this section will be approached in the same spirit and with' the same sense oi responsibility, looking to its being sparingly exercised and only in absolutely plain cases.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I understand, then, that the Government takes upon itself the responsibility of deciding as to the criminality of any published article?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: And that the court is only for the purpose of establishing the responsibility of the individual?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: No, I was speaking with reference to the suppression of the newspaper. When you come to the,prosecution against the individual, then you come to the court and the whole matter is fully opened.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
When a person is prosecuted because of an article published in a newspaper it is the character of that article, not himself personally, that is in question, and upon the character of that article he suffers the punishment provided in this section. What I was urging upon the Minister of Justice was that the suppression of a

newspaper, which 'is a very serious matter, indeed, should in the same way be made the subject of consideration by the court; that newspapers should not 'be suppressed unless an independent court had decided that the article published was in contravention of the terms of this section of the Act. I was claiming the same consideration for the property rights centred in the newspaper as is conceded to the individual in his personal rights-the right of trial and of evidence as to the facts. I see no reason why that cannot be done; I see every reason why it should be done.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I really do not think that it is practicable. In the cases to which I have referred it would hardly have been practicable for the Government to go to the courts for the purpose of obtaining a determination respecting the publications coming into the country from abroad or with regard to the newspaper which was suppressed tfor a certain time. The Government has never acted, nor would it propose to act, unless the case was so manifestly plain and beyond question that there could be ho doubt about it.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: The case of papers coming into the country is not at all on all fours with the case to which I am referring.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I think that it really is; I will tell my hon. friend why. In the case where a newspaper coming into this country in the ordinary course under postal convention is virtually suppressed by being refused admission, a question as to the action taken arises with the proprietors of the newspaper; sometimes it is made the subject of diplomatic inquiry. :So that the same question does arise, although the persons who publish the newspaper do not happen to be citizens of this country.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
That is what strikes me as constituting a great difference between the two cases. In the one case, we may do as we please, or as our neighbours will allow us; in the other, we are dealing with our own citizens and with investments of property very much out of proportion to the property affected by the suppression of the circulation of a paper coming into this country. The citizens of our country who have property rights in a newspaper are entitled to the benefit of every law that exists for the protection ' of their property; they are entitled to different consideration from that accorded to the citizens of any other country whose news papers may achieve some small circulation 213
here. I will mention another point of difference between this Act and the censorship or the stoppage of papers coming into this country from a foreign country. The censorship as it stands to-day is a censorship on account of treason or the giving of information of military value to the enemy. This is censorship directed against criticism of a government policy and administration-a different matter altogether. A discussion of the Government's policy and administration is essentially the right and business of every public newspaper in the country and the assumption of authority of the Government absolutely to destroy a newspaper without let or hindrance, without trial or consideration of any kind, is a very serious matter. I submit that that authority should not be assumed in the terms that the Prime Minister has laid down. Under the conditions which I have tri d to sketch, the right of the citizen in his property should he protected by proceedings before the courts.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I understand that if a paper transgresses it shall be summarily suppressed and shall remain suppressed for the duration of the war. As that is provided by Act of Parliament, I suppose that if a paper so suppressed should endaavour to make amends, apologize profusely and promise never to repeat the offence, that paper could only be reinstated by Act of Parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: On the suggestion of the member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) it was agreed that for the word " shall " we should substitute the word " may," to provide for possible limited duration of suspension.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: The Prime Minister intimated that the term might be for a period not exceeding the duration of the war.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
The application of the censorship in the past has, I am sorry to say, not been such as to inspire confidence in the good judgment or in the fair dealing of the Government in the administration of that censorship. We have the very startling instance of the suppression of a newspaper published at Sault Ste. Marie. I am' not aware of the grounds upon which that paper was suppressed. We are, however, aware that every week day since the war began there has been published in the city of Montreal a paper that, to my mind, has carried treasonable utterances in a large



majority of its issues, and it has not been touched hy the censor.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Why?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I cannot say why. I am only stating the fact, and the fact, according to my judgment, is such as to render the newspaper proprietors of this country very much alarmed at an enactment, proposed as this is, by which a paper, for criticism of the administration of this Government in regard to a matter which is of most intimate interest to the people of this country, is to be liable to arbitrary suppression. I am under the impression that no such law exists in any other country. In no other country are the newspapers placed under such conditions as to carrying on their business. That being the case, perhaps the Government has not yet considered the actual circumstances in regard to the newspaper business, the enormous amount of money invested in newspapers, the responsibilities that have to be carried by those who are concerned in their conduct and in connection with those investments, and-I am sorry to have to say it-the grave possibility of the power vested in tne Government by this section being used otherwise than on principles of absolute fair play and justice. The Government should systematically, for its own credit and for the cred:t of the country, absolutely avoid placing itself in a position where it could be accused of unfairness in the enforcement of this law. I am not objecting to the principle already stated, that when a law is passed it must be enforced and should be respected; but as to the provisions in regard to newspapers, I am compelled to think the Government has not had sufficient information as to the circumstances or conditions or it surely would not have framed this section in this form.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman kindly name the naper to which he refers, which ha?, pr'or to this date, been publishing seditious articles in the city of Montreal?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
The paper that is publishing articles that I consider have a very strong seditious tendency is Le Devoir.
Mr. MORPiHY: A French paper?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Yes, the paper that was largely responsible for the return of the present Government.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: When the hon. gentleman says that does he refer to articles published prior to 1911 or since?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Prior to 1911.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: He is complaining of the seditious character of articles written since 1911?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: The articles written since 1911 have, in large measure been, in my humble judgment, of a seditious character. Some hon. gentlemen asked why the discrimination between the paper published at Sault Ste. Marie and the paper published at Montreal. I want to be understood that I did not say that the failure to suppress the papeT in Montreal [DOT] was be-12 m. cause it had been largely instrumental in returning the present Government to power. I wish to draw attention to this far-reaching provision of this section, iby which not only is the paper that publishes an objectionable article suppressed, but another paper that copies that article is, if I understand the section correctly, automatically suppressed. Pei'haps those who drafted the section hardly realized how far-reaching that provision was. In the preparation of a newspaper, while the pen, now largely displaced by the typewriter, occupies a very important place, we will admit that the scissors are also used.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: In Edmonton.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: In using the exchanges for the purpose of providing matter for a paper, it is not the responsible editor who makes the selections, it is usually some subordinate member of the staff who does so, and I think it would be a most terrible thing that a paper should be absolutely suppressed because, through inadvertence, an objectionable article had appeared in its columns. Perhaps my hon. friend did not appreciate the technical points in that connection, or he surely would have thrown some saving provision around that penalty.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
I think the last observation is met by the substitution of the word " may " for the word " shall." The paper does not become absolutely suppressed, and I think circumstances such as the hon. gentleman mentions would have great weight in determining whether the paper that republishes should be suppressed or not. On the other hand, I think the hon. gentleman will admit that if would be a very foolish position to take to say: Well, the paper that contains the original article we will suppress, but all the other papers in the

country can print that article and keep it in circulation, and they will go on with impunity. I quite understand that the case the hon. gentleman suggests would not be a case for the exercise of the power, and his objection was very well taken so long as the imperative " shall " remained in the section, but the use of the word " may " would appeal to the judgment of anybody charged with the exercise of this power.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Carried.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
To the hon. members who are so anxious to have this section carried,
I say that this is the severest infraction of the rights of the people of Canada that has taken place since this Dominion wafj formed, and I do not think a few minutes are wasted in just going into the details of it.' A little while ago, the Prime Minister, if I understood him correctly, said that there was an absolute distinction between the offence of inciting opposition to the law and criticism of the law. There is a difference between the two things at the two extremes, but there is no sharp dividing line of difference between the two. No man can say definitely just where fair criticism ends and obstruction or interference, or incitement to interference begins.
If I say that the administration and legislation of this Government in a certain particular is wrong, I am thereby inciting people against that administration or legislation. I cannot criticise adversely the administration or legislation of the Government without in some degree inciting people to opposition to that administration or legislation ; and so I take the ground that when the Government introduces legislation worded in the general and comprehensive terms of these two sections, it is an attack upon free speech and upon the right and duty of public criticism of the public affairs of this country.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
There is some force in what my hon. friend says as to the two things shading into each other. The same observation is perfectly true as to the shading between what might legitimately be regirded as sedition and what might legitimately be regarded as the expression of a strong opinion not amounting to sedition. All that is perfectly true, but I do not see that it makes the provisions of the section unwise. We must deal with these things, and we simply have to exercise our best judgment as to whether a particular article is seditious or whether it is
something that is just a little short of being seditious.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I hope the committee will not be too weary, but my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) and myself are speaking for a very large and influential class of people in the community. What would the Government do in this case? Suppose a member of this House made a speech in this Chamber that would come under this Act if it appeared in a newspaper as an editorial. Would the newspaper be liable under this Act if it reproduced that speech?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I do not know.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: It is a matter of discretion.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I just wish to say a last word. From what the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice have just said, I can come to no other, conclusion than that from the passage of this Act forward the press of this country lies under threat from this Government, and to that extent is prevented from the exercise of the right and duty of legitimate criticism of the acts and administration of the Government.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
I should like to make one suggestion to the committee. Why not leave the question of press censorship, in so far as it is affected by this Bill in the hands of a judge of the Supreme Court. Extensive powers have been given to a judge of the Supreme Court by this Act. We come to one clause where there is absolutely no appeal of any kind, where there is not even a trial, and where the Government is taking upon itself to suppress a newspaper upon the judgment of one of its ministers. Now, there is a great difference, in my mind, between censorship after this law comes into force, and censorship as it has existed in the past. In the past censorship has been directed against sedition, against divulging secrets concerning the army, and so forth, but under these provisions it will be directed against 'any article which may-embarrass the Government in connection with the operation of this Act. That means that the Government is the interested party, the accuser, and also the judge. It certainly is against all principles of British justice to have the same man the accuser, the interested party, and the judge. I know that a lot of confidence is being placed under this Act in the judges of the Supreme Court. I believe the Government believe they will be absolutely fair

in the application of this Act. I feel sure that in the other clauses the Government have introduced all the safeguards they possibly could, and in this particular instance they are taking upon themselves a certain amount of authority that I am convinced at this time they will administer to the 'best of their knowledge and ability. But they are leaving people under the impression- this has been commonly stated in the few hours since these clauses have been printed -that they are taking this means of suppressing the Opposition press in the event of an election. I do not say that for a moment; I do not believe the Government would use the law for that purpose; but if they can remove that suspicion by placing the administration of this censorship in the hands of a judge of the Supreme Court, or some impartial body, why not do so, and avoid being at one and the same time accuser, judge and jury?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
I do not think my hon. friend has put it in quite the right light in one respect. He speaks of the Government being the accuser. It is really the state, the Government acting for the time being as its instrument, asserting the rights of the state against organized disobedience to the state's law; that is the position, nothing more and nothing less. Further than that, under the censorship which has had to be carried on not only in this country, but in Great Britain during the last three years Or thereabouts, powers quite as extensive as these have been capable of exercise, and, as I have said 'before, they have been very sparingly used-used almost altogether by suggestion to the press, by communication, and not by infliction of punishment whether in the way of suppression, prosecution, or otherwise. So I think there need be no serious apprehension about this. My hon. friend, however, has made a suggestion that is worthy of consideration. It is an invidious position for a Government to be in; I entirely agree with that. So far as the Government are concerned, we have left these matters altogether to the officers appointed, and have only interfered when the officers came to us for direction or with a recommendation. It has been left absolutely to the officers appointed, and so far as I know, and as I fully believe, they are animated by a desire to exercise their powers fairly and with perfect impartiality. The Government naturally would be sparing in the use of its powers in this connection, because whenever they are exercised those responsible are always open to un-[llr, Boivin.]
founded imputations and insinuations. My hon. friend says it might be proper that matters of this kind should be left to a judge of the Supreme Court. That is a suggestion which strikes me rather favourably at the moment, and I am prepared to consider it. If my hon. friend would be good enough to let the clause pass, I will undertake to return to it for the purpose of making the necessary amendment, or if we should not see fit to adopt the suggestion of my hon. friend, we will return to it for any purpose that may be desired.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: In case a paper is liable to be suppressed for treasonable editorials, would the editor be remonstrated with first? Would he be called before a judge of the Supreme Court, or before the board of censors, to explain or to amend, or would he simply be- summarily suppressed?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I think that will have to depend on the circumstances of the case. There may be some oases of so glaring a character 'that they would be beyond remonstrance, there might be other cases in which remonstration would be proper and desirable.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Suppose a paper is circulated publishing treasonable matter, would the editor be liable undeT subsection 2?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
He would not come
under the present subsection. He would come under the first part of subsection 5. Subsection 2 deals with verbal utterances, and 5 deals with printed or published utterances and adds the power of suppression in the case of printing.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Does the law reach only the editor, or does it reach the proprietor and those who finance the paper-the backers of the paper?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I think it does not go beyond those who have to do with the publication of the paper; those who are responsible for or take part in the publication of the treasonable matter. I do not think, for instance, the boy who tied up the newspaper bundles, or the .man who packed them for the purpose of sending them away, would be reached by this section.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
My hon. friend ha6 sufficient experience in journalism to know that very often the editor is only the instrument of other parties who finance the publication. Are those who are behind

the publication not as responsible as the editor himself?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
It would depend,
I suppose, on how they financed it. If they were really the proprietors and financed it in that way, they might be liable. If they were persons who financed the paper by lending money, they would not be liable because they lave really nothing to do with tlic direction of the paper.
Subsection agreed to on division.
On subsection 6 of proposed new section 16:
6. This section shall come into force on the day of the sanction of this Act.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: What is the meaning of the word "sanction" there?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: The Act is sanctioned when the Crown gives assent to it, that is to say the day the Act is finally passed.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Then, it is intended that the provisions of the section will be enforced between the time the Act is passed and the time it is proclaimed by the Government?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
As I understand
it merely means that after the Act has received the assent of the Governor General it shall not be competent to any person to urge disobedience of it. Its operation has not begun, so far as the calling out of men under it; it has not been proclaimed. But in the meantime it shall be unlawful for any person to urge disobedience of it.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I think it will be difficult to get a judge to convict a man for impeding the administration of an Act which is not being administered, and which has not yet come into force. This Act may be passed to-morrow, and it may be law as far as the assent of both Houses and the Governor General goes. Then it may not come into force by proclamation until the end of the year, or it may never come into force. Can we ask a judge to impose a penalty on a person for impeding the administration of an Act which is not in force and which may never come into force? You cannot stop a horse until you have started him. '

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: It is quite clear no one can impede an operation which operation is not going on, but people may advise and urge and arrange in advance to impede it when it comes into force. Under this section, we can reach them.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
I may inform my hon. friend the judge is only necessary to deal
with the individual. The Government can enforce the gag on the newspapers without any help from the judge.
Subsection agreed to on division.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
I expect the rearrangement of the clauses of the amendement moved as section 16 will make it clear that paragraph 6 applies only to paragraphs 2 and 5. It has not any application to the other paragraphs of the section. The second paragraph of section 17 must be retained. It may be made a separate section, as suggested by the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham).
There still remains section 3, which was left last night. That is the section which divides the men into classes. There were many who urged that it would be unfair to call class 1 ahead of classes 2 and 3, some urging that all three should be called together, and others urging that class 2 should precede class 1. Various reasons were given on both proposals. I stated that, while I felt it would be exceedingly inconvenient to call all three together and would result perhaps in impediments being thrown in the way of the operation of the Act, I would reserve the clause and consult with the other members of the Government. I desire now to recommend to the House that the three classes be united. At the same time, I wish to make it clear that we hope to get over the inconvenience that would result by calling them all together by such divisions in the regulations as may enable us to take care of them at times sufficiently separated to prevent congestion, and to ensure that all three will be treated absolutely alike in so far as priority of selection goes. It has been the intention to comb those first three classes at least, and more if required. That being the case I wish to move that clause 1 shall read as follows:
Those who have attained the age of twenty years and were born not earlier than the year 1883 and are unmarried or are widowers who have no child.
Then classes two and three would be struck out. There is no reason why classes one, two and three should be united that does not apply just as well to classes four, five and six. I therefore beg to move that class four be known as class two, and that its description read as follows:
Those who have attained the age of twenty years and were born not earlier than the year 1883 and are married or are widowers who have a child or children.
Classes five and six would then be struck out and the classes that are now classes seven, eight, nine and ten would be

changed to read classes three, four, five and six.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I would suggest that the last word in section three be changed from "youngest" to "oldest." The class ranges from twenty to thirty-four, and if they are not called out for another year the thirty-four year old man will certainly not be improved by waiting, while those who are of the age of twenty will be a year better at age twenty-one than they are at twenty.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: The intention, in fact the most absolute statement, is that no matter how they are called out there will be no priority as between those calls in the ages twenty to thirty-four. The arrangements for the trial of applications for exemptions will proceed in such a way that, all will be taken care of as nearly together as possible, so as not to congest the tribunals. Priority of obligation is abolished.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Is subsection 3 to be amended?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: No, it does not require to be amended.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: So long as the word "youngest" remains-

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: That is only the matter of the order of reporting, so long as you group the three, or are certain that all three are to be called, that priority is abolished.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: That is not the way the section reads. It says the order in which they are described in this (Section shall' be the order in which they are called out on active service.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Galled out is the proclamation, and we will say that the new Mass one is called out. A division is made in order to avoid congestion, and it is said that the first Mass will report on such a day and the second class on such another day and the third Mass on such another day. All of these must report. In so far as the applications for exemptions are concerned, we might have the tribunals sit on the last class first, but so far as this section goes, it is simply reporting to the military officers.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: 1 think there is more in it, than that. If you enlisted 100,000, under this the oldest man would be left off. I think it should be the youngest man.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
No, that would he a
matter for determination under the military rules that now exist. Any one can now be released. They could release the

oldest or the youngest, or one-half at the top and one-half at the bottom, if there were too many.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: Why not amend section 3?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: It would not affect that question; that is simply a question of the order of reporting.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext: I may not be here tomorrow. When the Prime Minister considers the section concerning the clergy, will he include the students in divinity and theoloey as they were considered in Washington when they passed a similar Bill? The term " Mergy " is a wide term and it might be well to mention students in divinity and theology.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF THE BILL IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE.
speechtext:
I shall take
that into consideration.
Progress reported.
On motion of Sir Robert Borden, the House adjourned at 12.40 a.m. Friday.
